meta.title: ML Engineer & Applied Scientist Roadmap
meta.subtitle: 19 levels across 7 phases — from software fundamentals to research & production

phases.name: Foundations
phases.goal: Build the engineering, computational, mathematical, and statistical foundations that every later level silently assumes. Nothing here is "preparation" to be rushed: a model that fails in production is usually failing because one of these four levels was skipped.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** you are allowed to move on when you can *build it* and *explain it*, not when you have *watched it*. Every module ends with a gate for exactly this reason.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk part-time · ~2× faster full-time
dashboard.core tools: VS Code, Git + GitHub, terminal, `uv`, `pytest`, NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Jupyter
dashboard.final outcome: Write reliable Python software, compute with NumPy/Pandas at speed, derive the maths behind ML models, and reason statistically about data and uncertainty.

levels.title: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING FUNDAMENTALS
levels.goal: Build the programming and software engineering skills needed to write, test, debug, and maintain real machine-learning code.
levels.mainProject: A tested, reusable **ML Data Quality Toolkit**

levels.title: PYTHON AND SCIENTIFIC COMPUTING
levels.goal: Move from "Python that runs" to "Python that computes correctly and fast": array thinking, tabular wrangling, numerical stability, visualisation, profiling, and reproducibility.
levels.mainProject: A **vectorised scientific computing library** with benchmarks

levels.title: MATHEMATICS FOR MACHINE LEARNING
levels.goal: Build the mathematical fluency to derive losses, read papers, debug optimisation, and answer "why does this work?" in an interview. You do not need to become a mathematician; you need to stop hand-waving.
levels.mainProject: **Maths Engine from Scratch** — a NumPy autodiff + PCA + optimisation library

levels.title: PROBABILITY AND STATISTICS
levels.goal: Go beyond formulas into statistical reasoning: model data with distributions, quantify uncertainty honestly, design experiments, and avoid the errors that make ML results irreproducible.
levels.mainProject: **Statistical Inference Toolkit** with a simulated experiment study

elements.text: **Purpose.** Prove the four levels work *together*. A single repository that ingests messy data, computes with vectorised code, models it with maths you implemented yourself, and reports results with correct uncertainty.
**Suggested duration.** 1–2 weeks **Depends on.** Levels 0, 1, 2, and 3.

Pick **one real question** answerable with a public dataset — ideally one you care about (credit default, hospital readmission, crop yield, exam performance, electricity demand, IPL outcomes, anything with a defensible outcome variable).
Then produce:

items.text: **A package** — not a notebook — that loads, validates, cleans, and models the data.
**A from-scratch estimator** — logistic or linear regression implemented with your own autodiff from Level 2, with gradients derived in the README.
**A statistical claim** — an effect, a difference, or a prediction with an interval attached, and the assumptions stated.
**A decision memo** — one page, written for someone who will act on the result.
**A reproducible report** — one command regenerates every number and figure.

rows: Schema checks, missingness report, duplicate detection, typed columns
No Python loops over rows; a benchmark table before/after
Trivial baseline, a library model, and your implementation, side by side
Bootstrap or analytic interval on every headline number
A small simulation showing your interval covers at the nominal rate
Recommendation, effect size, interval, cost, risks, and what would change the decision
Unit tests for data handling, model maths, and report generation
Format, lint, type-check, and tests run on every push
Install, run, results table, limitations, and one honest failure

elements.label: Pass mark
elements.value: At least 3 in every dimension, with **Correctness** and **Statistics** at 4 or above.

elements.text: You should be able to answer these without notes:

items.text: Which assumptions does your statistical claim rest on, and which are you least sure about?
What did your from-scratch implementation do differently from the library version, and why?
Where does your pipeline lose numerical precision?
What would happen to your conclusion if the sample were 10× smaller? 10× larger?
Which single number in your report are you least confident in?
If your effect is real but small, what would you recommend?

elements.text: If you are working and studying, stretch this to 20–24 weeks. The ordering matters; the calendar does not.

phases.name: Core ML
phases.themeLabel: EDA, feature engineering, classical ML, evaluation
phases.goal: Turn data into signal, signal into models, and models into evidence. This is the phase where most ML careers are actually decided: anyone can call `.fit()`, but very few people can prove a model generalises, explain why it fails, and defend a metric choice to a product team.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** a model is not done when it scores well. It is done when you can explain *why* it scores well, *where* it fails, and *what would happen* if the data changed.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk part-time · ~2× faster full-time
dashboard.main libraries: scikit-learn, Pandas, Polars, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, SHAP, Optuna, statsmodels
dashboard.final outcome: Build a leakage-audited pipeline, train and tune classical models, and prove generalisation with honest validation, calibrated probabilities, and error analysis.

levels.title: DATA ANALYSIS AND FEATURE ENGINEERING
levels.goal: Turn raw, messy, real-world data into features that are trustworthy, reproducible, and free of leakage — and know how to prove it.
levels.mainProject: A **leak-proof, versioned feature pipeline** with a data-quality report

levels.title: CLASSICAL MACHINE LEARNING
levels.goal: Master the models that still win on tabular data, and — more importantly — learn the modelling craft: baselines, bias–variance, regularisation, tuning, calibration, and interpretation.
levels.mainProject: A **tuned, calibrated, interpreted tabular model** that beats a strong baseline

levels.title: MODEL EVALUATION AND GENERALIZATION
levels.goal: Prove that a model will keep working on data it has never seen — and know exactly where it will not. This level converts "my model scored 0.91" into a defensible scientific claim.
levels.mainProject: A **generalization dossier**: protocol, metrics with intervals, error taxonomy, and slice analysis

capstone.title: Phase 2 Capstone: THE TABULAR DECISION SYSTEM

elements.text: **Purpose.** Compose Levels 4, 5, and 6 into one system: a leak-proof pipeline, a tuned and calibrated model, and an evaluation rigorous enough to put in front of a decision-maker.
**Suggested duration.** 1–2 weeks **Depends on.** Levels 4, 5, and 6.

Pick a real tabular problem with a genuine decision attached — credit risk, churn with a retention budget, hospital readmission with a care team, insurance claim triage, delivery-delay prediction, exam-outcome support. The domain matters less than the rigour.
Deliver a system that answers four questions:

items.text: **Is the data trustworthy?** (validation, leakage audit, point-in-time correctness)
**Is the model good?** (baselines, tuning, calibrated probabilities, untouched evaluation)
**Where does it fail?** (error taxonomy, worst-group, cost of those failures)
**What should the organisation do?** (threshold, expected value, monitoring plan)

rows: Six leak types checked; regression test in CI
Documented search, unbiased score from nested CV
Learning curves plus a stated next action
15+ slices with intervals and worst-group flagged
Cost matrix, threshold, expected value per 1,000 cases
Latency, model size, monitoring metrics, retraining trigger
One page, non-technical, with a recommendation

elements.label: Pass mark
elements.value: At least 3 in every dimension, with **Evaluation** and **Decision layer** at 4 or above.

items.text: What is your strongest evidence that this model will work on next month's data?
Which single assumption would, if false, invalidate your headline number?
What is your worst-performing slice, and what would you do about it?
Why this threshold and not the one that maximises F1?
How much does the model earn per 1,000 cases, and what is the interval on that estimate?
What would you monitor in the first week after launch?
If you had to halve the feature count tomorrow, what goes and what breaks?

I can encode high-cardinality features without leaking.
I can build point-in-time-correct temporal features.
I can name, detect, and prevent all six leakage types.
I can derive and interpret linear, logistic, and regularised models.
I can explain bagging and boosting from first principles.
I can tune with a documented protocol and report an unbiased score.
I can calibrate probabilities and measure calibration.
I can produce global and local explanations and state their limits.
I can define what my evaluation estimates and its assumptions.
I choose split strategies that match deployment.
I choose metrics and thresholds from a cost structure.
I compare models with paired tests and intervals.
I build error taxonomies and evaluate slices.
I attach calibrated uncertainty to predictions.
I can explain why offline gains may not ship.

elements.text: Answer these out loud, without notes. If any answer takes more than 60 seconds, revisit that level.

items.text: What is the grain of your data, and how did you verify it?
Name three ways your pipeline could leak, and the test that prevents each.
Why did you choose this model over the two you rejected?
What exactly does your AUC estimate, and what is its interval?
Where does your model fail worst, and how much does that cost?
Why is your threshold where it is?

elements.text: **Phase 2 is complete** when all four capstones pass and you can answer the eight questions above with numbers, not adjectives.

L4: feature engineering, encoding, temporal features
L4: leakage audit, imbalance, versioning **+ L4 capstone**

L5: model selection, interpretation, calibration **+ L5 capstone**
L6: comparison tests, slice analysis, error taxonomy

elements.text: Working full-time? Stretch to 16–18 weeks. Do not compress the evaluation weeks — they are the ones that change how you are perceived in interviews.

subBlocks.title: The 10 Most Common Ways to Fail Phase 2 (Core ML)

rows: Freeze the split and protocol first
Fit inside the fold via a pipeline
Random splits on temporal or grouped data
No idea whether a gain is real
PR-AUC, recall at fixed precision, cost-based threshold
Permutation importance and SHAP, with caveats
Tuning on 50 models and reporting the winner
Nested evaluation or a fresh holdout
You cannot say how it fails
Nobody can act on the model
Cost matrix, threshold, expected value per 1,000

phases.name: Deep Learning
phases.themeLabel: PyTorch bridge, backprop, training dynamics, architectures
phases.goal: Stop treating neural networks as a library call. Build one from scratch, understand why training succeeds or collapses, and learn to choose an architecture from evidence rather than fashion. By the end of this phase you can train, debug, ablate, and defend any deep model from an MLP to a transformer.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** a deep model is not "working" because the loss went down. It is working when you can explain the gradient path, the optimisation behaviour, and the ablation that justified each architectural choice.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk part-time · ~2× faster full-time
dashboard.main frameworks: PyTorch, `torch.autograd`, `einops`, Weights & Biases / MLflow, Hugging Face `transformers` (late L9)
dashboard.compute: One GPU strongly recommended (Colab/Kaggle free tiers are enough for every project here)
dashboard.entry requirement: The PyTorch readiness bridge in this document — unless you already train models in PyTorch
dashboard.final outcome: Implement autograd and backprop, diagnose any training failure from curves and gradients, and select, train, and ablate a modern architecture with measured evidence.

levels.title: PyTorch Readiness Bridge
levels.goal: Master tensors, nn.Module, the canonical training loop, DataLoaders, and device/precision discipline before starting Level 7.
levels.mainProject: torch-warmup — a working training loop you can explain

levels.title: NEURAL NETWORKS FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES
levels.goal: Build a neural network twice — once in NumPy with hand-derived gradients, once in PyTorch — and understand every line of the training loop. No `model.fit()`, no hidden magic.
levels.mainProject: **`mlp-lab`** — a NumPy MLP with manual backprop, matched against a PyTorch implementation

levels.title: OPTIMIZATION AND TRAINING DYNAMICS
levels.goal: Understand why deep networks train at all, why they stop training, and how to make training faster, more stable, and more reproducible. This is the level that separates people who tune by folklore from people who diagnose by mechanism.
levels.mainProject: **`dynamics-lab`** — an optimiser, schedule, and stability ablation study with a reproducible report

levels.title: DEEP LEARNING ARCHITECTURES
levels.goal: Learn the major architecture families well enough to choose one from evidence: convolutions, recurrence, attention, and generative designs. Then make them cheap enough to ship.
levels.mainProject: **`arch-zoo`** — five architectures, one task, one controlled comparison

elements.text: **Purpose.** Compose Levels 7, 8, and 9 into one system: a benchmark harness that trains multiple architectures under one protocol, with an ablation engine, a stability suite, and a report a reviewer can trust.
**Suggested duration.** 1–2 weeks **Depends on.** Levels 7, 8, and 9.
Build a benchmark suite that answers, for one task of your choosing:

items.text: **Which architecture wins** under equal parameters and under equal compute?
**Which training recipe** (optimiser, schedule, normalisation, precision) is best for each?
**Where does training break**, and which intervention restores stability?
**What does it cost** in parameters, FLOPs, latency, and memory?
**What would you ship**, and what did you reject?

elements.text: The domain is your choice: image classification, text classification, audio tagging, or a small generative task. The rigour is not optional.

rows: Committed before any experiment, with success criteria
Five families, each with parameter and FLOP counts
Matched-budget comparison, per-model tuned learning rate
One instability induced, three interventions compared
Every bug and unstable run, with cause and fix
Intended use, limits, metrics with intervals
One command rebuilds all tables and figures

phases.name: Advanced ML & Research
phases.goal: Move from training models to producing knowledge. Learn how representations are learned without labels, how advanced methods handle uncertainty, causality, sequences and shift, and how to design, execute, and communicate experiments that other people can trust. This is the phase that turns a strong engineer into an applied scientist.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** a result is not a result until someone else could reproduce it, and a method is not understood until you can name the assumption it breaks.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk part-time · ~2× faster full-time
dashboard.core tools: PyTorch, `timm`, Hugging Face `transformers`, `scikit-learn`, `statsmodels`, PyMC/`numpyro` (optional), `DoWhy`/`EconML`, `sktime`/`statsforecast`, `wandb`
dashboard.final outcome: Pretrain and evaluate representations, deploy at least two advanced methods correctly, and run a research-grade experiment that survives reproduction and review.

levels.title: REPRESENTATION AND SELF-SUPERVISED LEARNING
levels.goal: Understand how models learn useful features without labels, how to train such models on a modest budget, and how to prove the representation is actually good — with a frozen probe, not with vibes.
levels.mainProject: **`repr-lab`** — pretrain a small encoder with SSL, evaluate it frozen, and ablate the design

levels.title: ADVANCED ML METHODS
levels.goal: Add the methods that a senior applied scientist is expected to know but that Phase 2 does not cover: uncertainty, causality, sequences, recommendation, adaptation under shift, and constrained optimisation. You will implement two of them deeply rather than skim ten.
levels.mainProject: **`adv-ml-lab`** — two advanced methods implemented, benchmarked, and reported

levels.title: RESEARCH METHODS AND EXPERIMENTAL SCIENCE
levels.goal: Learn to produce knowledge, not just models: read papers critically, design experiments that can fail, reproduce results honestly, and write claims that your evidence actually supports.
levels.mainProject: **`research-repro`** — reproduce a published result, ablate it, and write a 4-page report

elements.text: **Purpose.** Run a complete mini research project end-to-end: a question, a protocol, an artefact, a result, a critique, and a paper-style writeup. This is the artefact that most directly predicts success in an applied-science interview.
**Suggested duration.** 2–3 weeks **Depends on.** Levels 10, 11, and 12.
Answer **one question** that you genuinely do not know the answer to, in a domain where you can obtain data and train small models.
Good sprint questions look like:

items.text: Does augmentation strength matter more than batch size for SSL on small datasets?
Do deep ensembles beat conformal prediction for triage in a cost-weighted setting?
Does a global forecaster beat per-series models when series are short and noisy?
Does the gain from a new architecture survive equal-FLOP tuning on my domain?
Does importance weighting help under a shift I can actually simulate?

elements.text: Bad sprint questions are broad ("how do transformers work?"), unmeasurable, or already settled by one obvious baseline.

rows: One sentence, falsifiable, with the baseline stated
Committed before experiments: metric, data, analysis, stopping rule
5–10 papers mapped, with the gap your question addresses
At least 3 configurations × 3 seeds, intervals reported
The claimed cause isolated; one control that shows no effect
What you would report if the effect vanished
Abstract, method, results, limitations, impact statement
A written review of your own work, as an adversary

Produce **one** of the following, in your chosen specialisation:

**Option B — Research thesis.** Produce a focused research contribution in your specialisation — a reproduction plus extension, a falsifying evaluation, a small method, or a new benchmark — with a workshop-style paper, artefact, and public release.
Both options must include the same rigour: pre-registration, intervals, seeds, compute reporting, honest failure analysis, and a reproducible artefact.

levels.title: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING FUNDAMENTALS
levels.goal: Build the programming and software engineering skills needed to write, test, debug, and maintain real machine-learning code.
levels.prerequisites: Basic computer use and willingness to learn programming. You do not need previous ML knowledge.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)

sections.title: Python Core
sections.objective: Become comfortable writing Python programs without depending on tutorials for every step.

items.text: Understand variables and assignment, and what a name actually points to.
Learn integers, floats, strings, booleans, and the difference between `int` and `float` division.
Understand type conversion (`int()`, `float()`, `str()`, `bool()`) and when it silently loses information.
Use arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators, including operator precedence.
Understand `None` and truthy/falsy values (`0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}` are falsy — know why that matters in `if`).
Use `if`, `elif`, and `else`, including nested and chained comparisons.
Use `for` and `while` loops; iterate over ranges, strings, lists, and dictionaries.
Understand `break`, `continue`, `pass`, and `range()` with start/stop/step.
Use `input()` and formatted strings — f-strings, format specifiers such as `{value:.2f}`.
Read error messages and understand basic exceptions (`NameError`, `TypeError`, `ValueError`, `IndexError`).
Write a program to check whether a number is prime.
Build a number-guessing game with attempt counting and input validation.
Calculate the mean, minimum, and maximum of a list without using `statistics`.
Count vowels, words, and characters in a string.
Build a simple menu-driven calculator that loops until the user quits.
**Lists:** indexing, slicing, insertion, deletion, sorting, reversing, and `sort` versus `sorted`.
**Tuples:** immutability, unpacking, and using tuples as dictionary keys.
**Dictionaries:** keys, values, lookup, update, iteration, `get`, and `setdefault`.
**Sets:** uniqueness, membership tests, unions, intersections, and differences.
**Strings:** common methods, slicing, joining, splitting, and formatting.
List, dictionary, and set comprehensions — including when a loop is more readable.
Nested data structures: lists of dicts, dicts of lists, and how to navigate them.
Mutable versus immutable objects, and why tuples can be hashable while lists cannot.
Object references: the difference between copying, shallow copying, and aliasing.
Basic iterator and generator concepts; the difference between a list and a generator.
Count the frequency of words in a text and report the top 10.
Find duplicates in a list — once with a set, once preserving order.
Group student records by department using a dictionary.
Sort records by multiple fields (for example, department ascending, score descending).
Remove duplicates from a list while preserving order, and explain the complexity.
Process a list of dictionaries representing dataset records: filter, transform, aggregate.
Define and call functions; understand parameters and return values.
Use positional and keyword arguments, and know when keyword arguments improve clarity.
Understand default arguments and the danger of mutable defaults such as `def f(x, acc=[])`.
Use `*args` and `**kwargs` to write flexible wrappers.
Understand local, enclosing, global, and built-in scope (the LEGB rule).
Write docstrings that state inputs, outputs, and raised exceptions.
Learn type hints, including `list[str]`, `dict[str, float]`, and `Optional`.
Understand pure functions and side effects; prefer pure functions inside data pipelines.
Break large problems into small functions with one reason to change.
Write reusable functions for mean, median, variance, and standard deviation.
Write a function that validates a dataset's column names against a required list.
Build a reusable input-validation function used by three different scripts.
Refactor a long (100+ line) program into smaller functions with a clear call graph.
Read and write text files, and understand encoding problems with non-ASCII text.
Use context managers with `with` so files close even when an error occurs.
Work with CSV and JSON files using `csv` and `json`, and know their limitations.
Work with file paths using `pathlib` instead of string concatenation.
Handle exceptions with `try`, `except`, `else`, and `finally`.
Raise appropriate exceptions using `raise`, with informative messages.
Distinguish invalid user input (expected, recoverable) from programming errors (bugs).
Avoid silently swallowing exceptions with bare `except:`.
Read a CSV file and summarize its contents (rows, columns, missing values per column).
Save program output to JSON with a stable key order.
Handle missing files gracefully and return a helpful message instead of a traceback.
Validate JSON input and report which record is malformed and why.
Create a program that logs invalid records and continues processing the rest.
Convert a problem statement into smaller steps before writing code.
Write pseudocode before implementing complex logic.
Test normal cases, edge cases, and invalid inputs.
Trace code manually — variables, values, and state — instead of guessing.
Explain *why* a solution works, not only *what* it does.
Compare two solutions for clarity and performance.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.1).** Solve at least **15 small Python problems independently**. Be able to explain your code without re-reading a tutorial.

sections.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
sections.objective: Understand how to organise data and solve programming problems efficiently.

items.text: Understand what an algorithm is and what makes one better than another.
Learn time complexity and count operations rather than wall-clock seconds.
Learn space complexity, including the cost of building intermediate lists.
Understand Big-O notation and why constants are dropped.
Analyse single loops, nested loops, and loops whose range shrinks each iteration.
Understand the **average** cost of dictionary and set operations ($O(1)$ average, $O(n)$ worst case).
Learn why algorithm choice dominates micro-optimisations at large $n$.

elements.title: Practice
elements.subtitle: For five functions you have already written, state the complexity and one input size where it would become a problem.

items.text: For five functions you have already written, state the complexity and one input size where it would become a problem.
Arrays and Python lists: contiguous storage, indexing, amortised append cost.
Strings and string-processing patterns: building output with `join`, not `+=` in a loop.
Hash maps and hash sets: what a hash function does and why collisions matter.
Stacks (LIFO) and queues (FIFO), and the cost of `pop(0)` on a list.
Linked-list concepts: nodes, pointers, traversal, and why Python rarely uses them.
Heaps and priority queues via `heapq`; when a heap beats sorting.
Trees and binary search trees: ordering property, depth, and balancing intuition.
Graph fundamentals: nodes, edges, directed versus undirected, adjacency list representation.
Linear search versus binary search, and the sorted-input requirement of the latter.
Sorting algorithms and their trade-offs: insertion, merge, quick, and Python's Timsort.
Two-pointer technique on sorted arrays and strings.
Sliding-window technique for contiguous-subarray problems.
Frequency counting with dictionaries and `collections.Counter`.
Recursion, base cases, and recursion depth limits.
Tree traversal: pre-order, in-order, post-order, BFS by level.
Graph traversal: DFS and BFS, visited sets, and cycle detection.
Basic greedy algorithms and when greedy is *wrong*.
Introductory dynamic programming: overlapping subproblems and memoisation.

elements.text: Complete approximately **25–35 carefully selected problems**:

items.text: 5 problems on arrays and strings.
5 problems on dictionaries and sets.
5 problems on sorting and searching.
5 problems on stacks, queues, or heaps.
5 problems on recursion, trees, or graphs.
5 additional problems targeting your weakest areas.

elements.text: For every problem, record:

items.text: The simplest correct approach.
The improved approach, if one exists.
Time and space complexity.
Edge cases considered.
Why the solution works, in two sentences.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.2).** Solve common easy-level problems independently and make a reasonable attempt at intermediate problems. You should be able to **discuss complexity**, not merely produce code.

sections.title: Modules, Object-Oriented Programming, and Project Structure
sections.objective: Move from writing isolated scripts to building reusable software.

items.text: Understand Python modules and how `import` resolves names.
Import functions and classes correctly, including `from x import y as z`.
Understand the purpose of `__init__.py` in modern (namespace-aware) Python.
Separate application code from utility functions.
Understand Python's module search path at a basic level (`sys.path`).
Use the `if __name__ == "__main__":` pattern to separate library code from scripts.
Avoid circular imports by moving shared types into a common module.
Design a clear folder structure that a stranger can navigate.
Understand classes and objects as blueprints and instances.
Define attributes and methods; understand `self` and `__init__`.
Learn instance attributes versus class attributes, and the shared-mutable bug.
Understand encapsulation: what should be private and what should be public.
Learn inheritance and composition — and why composition is usually the safer default.
Understand polymorphism through a shared interface (duck typing).
Recognise when a simple function is better than a class.
Learn useful special methods such as `__repr__`, `__eq__`, and `__len__`.
Understand dataclasses and when they replace boilerplate classes.
Separate responsibilities between modules: loading, validating, computing, reporting.
Avoid repeated code without creating premature abstractions.
Design functions with clear inputs, documented outputs, and no hidden global state.
Keep configuration separate from application logic.
Understand basic separation of concerns.
Recognise tightly coupled code and the symptoms (one change breaks five files).
Learn basic dependency injection: pass collaborators in rather than constructing them inside.
Design errors and return values consistently across the project.
Add type hints to public functions and important internal ones.
Use `Optional`/`| None` and union types where a value may be absent.
Understand basic generic types such as `list[str]` and `dict[str, float]`.
Write useful docstrings that state purpose, parameters, returns, and raises.
Document expected inputs and outputs, including shapes and units.
Document exceptions a function may raise.
Learn the basics of static type checking with `mypy` and understand that hints do not enforce anything at runtime.

ml_data_tools/

    ├── test_validation.py
    └── test_statistics.py

items.text: Load a CSV file from a path.
Check that required columns exist and report the missing ones.
Validate basic data types per column.
Calculate summary statistics for numeric columns.
Raise clear, custom errors for invalid data.
Separate each responsibility into a suitable module.
Add type hints and docstrings.
Write a README with usage examples.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.3).** A user can `import` your package and call its functions without copying code out of your notebook.

sections.title: Git and GitHub
sections.objective: Track changes, collaborate safely, and maintain a professional project repository.

items.text: Understand repositories and the three areas: working directory, staging area, commit history.
Use `git init` and `git clone`.
Use `git status`, `git add`, and `git commit` with meaningful messages.
Inspect changes using `git diff` and `git diff --staged`.
Read commit history using `git log --oneline --graph`.
Understand `.gitignore` and why data, environments, and secrets stay out of history.
Learn branches, switching, and merging.
Resolve basic merge conflicts by reading the markers.
Undo changes safely: `restore`, `checkout`, and `stash`.
Understand the difference between `revert` (history-preserving) and `reset` (history-rewriting).
Create a GitHub repository and connect a local remote.
Push and pull changes, and understand what a rejected push means.
Open and review pull requests; give and receive review comments.
Understand issues, labels, and project boards.
Write a clear README with installation, usage, and limitations.
Use tags and releases at a basic level.
Understand GitHub Actions conceptually — workflows, jobs, and steps.
Never commit passwords, API keys, tokens, or private credentials.
Create a repository for your data validation package.
Make changes through a feature branch.
Write clear commits that each do one thing.
Open and merge a pull request.
Resolve a deliberately created merge conflict in a practice repository.
Document installation and usage.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.4).** You can manage your project history without losing work and explain the purpose of each main Git operation.

sections.title: Debugging, Logging, and Testing
sections.objective: Learn how to prove that your code works and diagnose why it fails.

items.text: Read Python tracebacks from the **bottom upward**, starting at the last frame in your code.
Distinguish syntax errors, runtime errors, and logical errors.
Use breakpoints and the debugger instead of adding `print` everywhere.
Inspect variables, call stack, and expressions during execution.
Reproduce a bug with a minimal example before attempting a fix.
Check assumptions about input shapes, types, and units.
Use `assert` for internal invariants that must never be false.
Investigate errors instead of applying random fixes and hoping.
Learn the Python `logging` module: loggers, handlers, formatters, levels.
Understand DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL, and choose levels deliberately.
Log important program events: start, inputs summary, decisions, completion, counts.
Include useful context — file name, row number, record ID — in messages.
Avoid logging secrets, credentials, or personal data.
Understand why `print()` is not a complete logging strategy (no levels, no rotation, no timestamps).
Write your first pytest test and run it from the terminal.
Test functions independently, in isolation from external systems.
Use plain `assert` statements and understand pytest's failure output.
Test exceptions with `pytest.raises`.
Parameterise tests with `@pytest.mark.parametrize` to cover many cases cheaply.
Use fixtures for shared setup and teardown.
Test edge cases and invalid inputs, not only the happy path.
Understand test isolation and why global state breaks it.
Learn mocking at a basic level with `monkeypatch` or `unittest.mock`.
Measure coverage with `pytest --cov` without treating coverage as proof of correctness.
Test empty datasets and empty files.
Test missing columns and unexpected extra columns.
Test duplicate rows and duplicate index values.
Test invalid numeric values, mixed types, and strings in numeric columns.
Test unexpected data types and schema drift.
Test missing-value handling, including all-missing columns.
Test that output schemas are consistent across runs.
Test that invalid inputs produce clear, actionable errors.

modules.title: Break and repair a data-processing pipeline

items.text: Write a simple CSV processing script (load → clean → aggregate → write).
Introduce **five different bugs**: an off-by-one filter, a wrong column, a silent type coercion, a mishandled missing value, and a unit error.
Reproduce each bug with a minimal example.
Write tests that detect each failure.
Fix the bugs.
Add regression tests that prevent the same errors from returning.
Document what caused each problem and how you found it.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.5).** You can demonstrate a bug, explain its cause, fix it, and show a test that would catch it in the future.

sections.title: Command Line and Linux Basics
sections.objective: Become comfortable working outside an IDE, running scripts, and managing files and processes.

items.text: Navigate directories using `pwd`, `cd`, and `ls` (including `ls -la`).
Create and remove files and directories (`mkdir`, `touch`, `rm`, `rmdir`).
Copy and move files (`cp`, `mv`).
Read files using `cat`, `less`, `head`, and `tail -f` for logs.
Search file contents using `grep`, including `grep -r` and `grep -n`.
Find files using `find` and `fd`.
Redirect output with `>`, `>>`, and `2>`, and suppress with `/dev/null`.
Understand pipes and chain commands (`grep | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`).
Use environment variables and `export`.
Run Python scripts from a terminal and pass arguments with `argparse`.
Understand process IDs and basic process management (`ps`, `top`, `kill`).
Understand file permissions, `chmod`, and why `chmod +x` is needed for scripts.
Learn basic shell scripting with variables, conditionals, and exit codes.
Understand absolute versus relative paths, and `.` and `..`.
Recognise exit codes and command failures when a program returns a non-zero status.
Run your package's tests from the terminal.
Write a script that processes a CSV file passed as a command-line argument.
Save program logs to a file and tail them while the program runs.
Search a project for a specific function name or error message with `grep -rn`.
Write a shell script that runs tests and reports failure with a non-zero exit code.
Understand the basics of using a remote Linux machine over SSH.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.6).** You can run, test, and troubleshoot a Python project without relying on IDE buttons.

sections.title: Environments and Dependency Management
sections.objective: Make your code reproducible on another computer — including future-you.

items.text: Understand Python versions and package versions, and why both matter.
Create virtual environments with `venv` (and know why system Python is off-limits).
Activate and deactivate an environment, and verify which interpreter is active.
Install packages with `pip`, or manage projects with `uv` for speed and lockfiles.
Understand `requirements.txt` and its limitations.
Learn the basics of `pyproject.toml`: project metadata, dependencies, build system.
Understand dependency constraints (`==`, `>=`, `~=`) and the risk of unbounded ranges.
Separate runtime dependencies from development dependencies.
Install your own package in editable mode (`pip install -e .`).
Understand environment variables and configuration files for settings.
Keep secrets outside source code, using `.env` files that are git-ignored.
Recreate an environment from documented dependencies on a clean machine.
Diagnose package version conflicts by reading resolver output.
Understand why reproducibility matters for experiments and audits.
Create a fresh environment from scratch.
Install your package and its dependencies using only your written instructions.
Run all tests.
Follow your own README as if you were a stranger.
Record and fix any missing installation steps.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.7).** Another developer can reproduce your development environment using your instructions alone.

sections.title: HTTP, REST APIs, and JSON
sections.objective: Learn the basics of connecting software components. You will use these skills later to serve ML predictions through APIs.

items.text: Understand clients and servers, and the request/response model.
Learn HTTP requests and responses: method, URL, headers, body, status.
Understand GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE, and the idea of idempotency.
Learn common HTTP status codes: 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 422, 429, 500.
Understand JSON objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and `null`.
Send requests using Python's `requests` library and inspect the response object.
Parse JSON responses and handle malformed or missing fields.
Handle network errors, timeouts, and retries at a basic level.
Validate incoming data before using it.
Understand basic REST API design: resources, endpoints, and consistent naming.
Learn what authentication is: API keys, bearer tokens, and headers.
Understand why API keys should never be committed to Git.
Recognise basic API input-validation and error-handling patterns.

items.text: An endpoint that accepts dataset information (rows, columns, types).
Request validation with Pydantic models.
A JSON summary response: counts, missing percentages, per-column types.
Appropriate error responses with clear messages.
Tests for valid and invalid requests.
Generated documentation at `/docs`.
Run the service locally and send requests to it with `curl` and `requests`.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.8).** You can explain how a client sends data to a service and how the service validates and returns a response.

sections.title: Code Quality and Professional Development Practices
sections.objective: Bring the previous skills together into code that is easy to maintain.

modules.title: Code Quality and Professional Development Practices

items.text: Follow consistent Python naming conventions (PEP 8): `snake_case`, `PascalCase`, `UPPER_CASE`.
Write short, focused functions with one reason to change.
Avoid unnecessary duplication — but do not abstract two similar lines prematurely.
Use type hints consistently across the public surface.
Write meaningful docstrings, not restatements of the function name.
Format code using **Ruff** (or Black) and let the tool settle style arguments.
Run lint checks and fix warnings rather than disabling them.
Separate configuration from implementation.
Use structured logging rather than scattered `print`.
Write meaningful tests that assert behaviour, not implementation details.
Understand basic code review: read the diff, ask questions, verify behaviour.
Review code for readability and maintainability, not only correctness.
Add a continuous integration workflow that runs format, lint, type-check, and tests.
Document installation, usage, and known limitations.
Make project execution reproducible from a single documented command.
Understand the basics of software licensing and third-party dependency risk.
The project installs from documented instructions.
Tests run successfully from the command line.
Formatting and lint checks pass.
Invalid inputs are handled clearly.
No secrets are stored in the repository.
The README includes a working example.
The repository contains no unnecessary generated files.
A fresh user can understand the project structure.
