elements.text: **Level 4 completion rule.** If you can hand a teammate your feature matrix, its dictionary, and its audit — and they can rebuild it without you — you are ready for Level 5.

levels.title: CLASSICAL MACHINE LEARNING
levels.goal: Master the models that still win on tabular data, and — more importantly — learn the modelling craft: baselines, bias–variance, regularisation, tuning, calibration, and interpretation.
levels.prerequisites: Level 4. You need a leak-proof feature pipeline before tuning anything — otherwise you will tune your way into a leak.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, statsmodels, Optuna, SHAP
dashboard.main project: A **tuned, calibrated, interpreted tabular model** that beats a strong baseline
dashboard.final outcome: Choose, train, tune, and explain classical models, and justify every choice with measured evidence.

sections.title: Framing the Learning Problem
sections.objective: Translate a business question into a prediction task that can actually be measured.

items.text: What decision will this model change? If nothing, do not build it.
The prediction unit, the label definition, and the horizon.
Who acts on the output, how often, and with what latency budget.
The cost of each error type, and who bears it.
The feedback loop: how will you learn whether the prediction was right?
Take three business questions and rewrite each as a labelled prediction task with a horizon.
Write the cost matrix for one of them, with actual numbers.
Supervised: classification, regression, ranking, survival, and structured prediction.
Unsupervised: clustering, density estimation, dimensionality reduction.
Self-supervised and transfer settings (preview of Levels 9–10).
When the task is really causal, and a predictive model will mislead you.
When ML is the wrong tool: deterministic rules, tiny data, or no feedback.
For six product problems, name the learning setting and justify it in one line.
Identify one problem where a rule beats a model, and explain why.
Trivial baselines: majority class, mean/median, last value, popularity, random.
Simple baselines: logistic regression, a shallow tree, a heuristic rule.
Why the baseline is the reference against which all lift is measured.
Recording baseline metrics with intervals, not point estimates.
The "beat the baseline or explain why not" rule.
Build three baselines for a classification task and report metrics with intervals.
Show a case where a tuned model fails to beat the baseline, and diagnose why.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.1).** You can state the decision, the label, the horizon, the cost matrix, and the baseline before training anything.

sections.title: Linear Models
sections.objective: Understand the workhorse models deeply enough to know exactly when they fail.

items.text: OLS assumptions and what breaks each one.
Coefficient interpretation, including units and interaction terms.
Residual diagnostics: patterns, heteroscedasticity, non-linearity.
Influence: leverage and Cook's distance.
Why extrapolation is unsafe with a linear model.
Fit a model, plot residuals, and identify two assumption violations.
Construct a dataset where a unit change in $x$ does not correspond to a unit change in $y$, and explain the coefficient anyway.
Ridge: shrinkage, stabilising collinear features, closed form.
Lasso: sparsity, feature selection, and the geometry behind it.
Elastic Net: when features are correlated in groups.
Standardisation before penalisation — and why it is mandatory.
The regularisation path and choosing $\lambda$ by cross-validation.
Plot the coefficient path for lasso across $\lambda$ and interpret it.
Show ridge outperforming OLS on collinear features in a held-out set.
Log-odds, sigmoid, and maximum likelihood.
Coefficient interpretation as odds ratios.
Class weights, offsets, and varying base rates.
Separation and its fix (regularisation).
Why logistic regression remains a strong, calibrated, explainable baseline.
Fit logistic regression by hand (gradient descent) and match `sklearn`.
Show complete separation producing enormous coefficients, then fix it with $L_2$.
The exponential family and the link function.
Poisson regression for counts; exposure offsets.
Negative binomial for overdispersed counts.
Gamma and Tweedie for cost and insurance-style targets.
Why using linear regression on counts or costs is usually wrong.
Fit Poisson and negative binomial models to the same count data and compare fit.
Show a Tweedie model beating squared-error regression on a zero-inflated cost target.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.2).** You can derive, fit, interpret, and diagnose a linear or logistic model without a library hiding anything.

sections.title: Distance-Based and Probabilistic Models
sections.objective: Understand memorisation-based learning and its geometric limits.

items.text: Distance metrics and the need for scaling.
Choosing $k$: bias–variance trade-off.
Weighted voting and distance weighting.
The curse of dimensionality and distance concentration.
Search structures: KD-trees, ball trees, approximate indexes.
Show k-NN accuracy collapsing as dimensions increase at fixed $n$.
Compare KD-tree and brute-force search at 10,000 and 1,000,000 points.
Conditional independence and why it is wrong but useful.
Multinomial NB for counts; Gaussian NB for continuous features.
Laplace smoothing and its effect on rare categories.
Why NB is a strong text baseline despite its assumptions.
Build a text classifier with NB and compare against logistic regression on TF-IDF.
Show NB's probabilities are poorly calibrated even when ranking is good.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.3).** You can explain when distance or independence assumptions are reasonable — and when they will silently fail.

sections.title: Support Vector Machines and Kernels
sections.objective: Understand margins, the kernel trick, and convex optimisation in a model you can actually use.

items.text: Maximum-margin classifiers and support vectors.
Hard versus soft margins; the role of $C$.
Hinge loss and its relationship to logistic loss.
The dual formulation and why it enables kernels.
Kernels: linear, polynomial, RBF; the $\gamma$ parameter.
Computational cost: $O(n^2)$–$O(n^3)$ training; when SVMs stop being practical.
Scaling and why SVMs need standardised inputs.
Kernel approximation (Nyström, random features) for large data.
Train linear, polynomial, and RBF SVMs on the same data and compare the decision boundary shape.
Show the effect of $C$ and $\gamma$ on overfitting with a validation curve.
Measure training time versus $n$ and identify where it becomes impractical.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.4).** You can explain the margin, the kernel trick, and the cost curve, and choose an SVM only when it is the right tool.

sections.title: Trees and Ensembles
sections.objective: Master the models that win on tabular data — and understand precisely why.

items.text: Recursive partitioning and greedy split selection.
Impurity criteria: Gini, entropy, and variance for regression.
Depth, minimum samples, and pruning.
Why single trees overfit and are unstable.
Interpreting a tree and its limitations.
Grow a tree by hand on a toy dataset and compute the Gini gain for two candidate splits.
Show that changing five rows changes the tree structure completely.
Bootstrap aggregation and variance reduction.
Feature subsampling and decorrelation of trees.
Out-of-bag error as a free validation estimate.
Hyperparameters: number of trees, max depth, max features, min samples leaf.
Why random forests rarely overfit with more trees, and what still does.
Plot OOB error against the number of trees and explain the plateau.
Show the effect of `max_features` on correlation between trees and on accuracy.
Stagewise additive modelling: each tree fits the current residual.
Functional gradient descent and the role of the learning rate.
Shrinkage, subsampling, and early stopping.
Tree constraints: depth, leaves, min child weight, $\gamma$.
Regularisation: $L_1$/$L_2$ on leaf weights.
Why boosting reduces bias while bagging reduces variance.
Implement a 50-line gradient booster for squared error and compare with a library.
Show the effect of learning rate × number of trees on validation error.
Demonstrate early stopping preventing overfitting on a noisy dataset.
Histogram-based splits and their speed advantage.
Leaf-wise versus level-wise growth.
Native categorical handling (CatBoost ordered target statistics, LightGBM categorical splits).
Missing-value handling by default direction.
Practical hyperparameter order: learning rate → trees → depth/leaves → sampling → regularisation.
GPU training and when it helps.
Train all three on the same dataset with sensible defaults and compare score, time, and model size.
Tune one of them with a documented search order and report the gain at each step.
Stacking with out-of-fold predictions to avoid leakage.
Level-1 meta-models: linear, ridge, or shallow trees.
Blending versus stacking; when the gain justifies complexity.
Diversity as the source of ensemble gain.
The interpretability and maintenance cost of an ensemble.
Stack logistic regression, random forest, and LightGBM with out-of-fold predictions.
Show that stacking two nearly identical models adds nothing.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.5).** You can tune a gradient-boosted model systematically, explain each hyperparameter's effect, and justify why you did not use a neural network.

sections.title: Unsupervised Learning
sections.objective: Find structure without labels — and know when the structure is real.

items.text: k-means: objective, Lloyd's algorithm, initialisation, and $k$ selection.
Gaussian mixtures and EM: soft assignments and covariance shapes.
DBSCAN and HDBSCAN: density, noise points, and no need for $k$.
Hierarchical clustering and linkage choices.
Validation: silhouette, Davies–Bouldin, Calinski–Harabasz, stability across seeds.
The real test: are the clusters actionable?
Cluster a dataset with three methods and compare assignments with adjusted Rand index.
Show k-means failing on non-spherical clusters that DBSCAN handles.
Check cluster stability across ten seeds and report which clusters persist.
PCA: variance maximisation, component interpretation, and scaling.
Explained variance and choosing the number of components.
t-SNE: local structure, perplexity, and why distances between clusters are meaningless.
UMAP: speed, global structure, and parameter sensitivity.
When to use PCA as preprocessing versus visualisation only.
Reduce a dataset to 2D with PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP; compare what structure survives.
Show how changing perplexity changes t-SNE's apparent clusters.
Isolation forest, local outlier factor, one-class SVM.
Reconstruction-error approaches with autoencoders (preview).
Supervised versus unsupervised framing when labels exist for some anomalies.
Threshold selection and alert budget.
Evaluation without labels: injection tests and expert review.
Inject known anomalies into clean data and measure detection at a fixed alert rate.
Compare three detectors' precision–recall trade-offs.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.6).** You can cluster, reduce, or detect anomalies with a method you can justify, and show the result is stable and useful.

sections.title: Hyperparameter Optimisation
sections.objective: Search efficiently, and never tune on the data you report.

items.text: Grid search and its exponential cost.
Random search and why it beats grid in high dimensions.
Bayesian optimisation: surrogate models and acquisition functions.
Hyperband and successive halving for early stopping of bad trials.
Population-based training at a conceptual level.
Optuna study design: pruners, samplers, and search spaces.
Run grid, random, and Bayesian search with the same budget; compare best score versus trials used.
Add a pruner and show it saves at least 40% of compute.
Why tuning and reporting on the same folds inflates results.
Inner loop for hyperparameters, outer loop for honest evaluation.
Grouped and time-series variants.
The cost of nested CV and when a holdout is sufficient.
Reporting the variance of the outer-fold scores.
Compare a naive tuned score with a nested-CV score on the same data; quantify the optimism.
Run nested CV with grouped splits and explain the difference.
Fix the validation protocol before searching.
Change one thing at a time and record the delta.
Prefer defaults first, then coarse ranges, then fine ranges.
Watch the interaction between learning rate and tree count.
Know when tuning has hit diminishing returns.
Log every trial with config, score, and runtime.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.7).** You can run a search with a documented protocol and report an unbiased score from nested validation.

sections.title: Model Selection and Comparison
sections.objective: Choose a model for reasons you can defend, not for a decimal place.

items.text: Compare against a baseline and against the previous production model.
Report mean and spread across folds — never a single number.
Statistical comparison: paired tests across folds, corrected resampled $t$-test.
Practical significance: is a 0.3-point AUC gain worth 3× inference cost?
Operational constraints: latency, memory, model size, retraining time, explainability.
Simplicity preference: choose the simpler model unless the gain is real and needed.

sections.title: Interpretability
sections.objective: Explain a model honestly, including where the explanation lies.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.9).** You can produce a global and a local explanation, state their assumptions, and identify one case where the explanation is misleading.

sections.title: Probability Calibration
sections.objective: Make predicted probabilities mean what they say.

Reliability diagrams and expected calibration error.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (5.10).** Your reported probabilities match observed frequencies within a stated tolerance, across the segments you care about.

subBlocks.title: Project: `tabular-arena` — a tuned, calibrated, interpreted classifier or regressor

One case where the explanation would mislead a stakeholder.

A lift-at-top-decile table.

levels.title: MODEL EVALUATION AND GENERALIZATION
levels.goal: Prove that a model will keep working on data it has never seen — and know exactly where it will not. This level converts "my model scored 0.91" into a defensible scientific claim.
levels.prerequisites: Levels 3–5. You need statistics (intervals, tests), modelling (baselines, tuning), and a feature pipeline that does not leak.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: scikit-learn model selection, statsmodels, SciPy, `mapie` (conformal), SHAP, your L3 toolkit

sections.title: The Generalization Problem
sections.objective: Understand precisely what a test score estimates, and why it is noisier than it looks.

modules.title: Empirical risk and the true objective

When to prefer a large holdout over nested CV.
Reporting the protocol so it can be reproduced.
Run nested CV with a 20-trial search and compare with a naively tuned score.

sections.title: Classification Metrics and Thresholds

modules.title: The confusion matrix and derived metrics

items.text: True/false positives and negatives, and the four rates that matter.

Balanced accuracy and macro/micro/weighted averaging.

Compute all metrics for a fixed threshold and show two models with identical accuracy and different behaviour.

Precision–recall curves and PR-AUC under class imbalance.
The base-rate effect on precision.
Lift and cumulative gains for targeting.
Kendall's insight: AUC is a ranking probability.
Show two models with equal AUC but very different PR curves.
Demonstrate how precision at a fixed recall changes when the base rate drops 10×.
Expected-cost minimisation with a cost matrix.
Capacity constraints: human review bandwidth, contact limits, budgets.
Operating points and why the default 0.5 is arbitrary.

Demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalised odds, predictive parity.

Base-rate differences and why they create tension.
Choosing a criterion from the decision context and the legal setting.

sections.title: Uncertainty in Predictions

levels.title: PyTorch Readiness Bridge
levels.goal: Master tensors, nn.Module, the canonical training loop, DataLoaders, and device/precision discipline before starting Level 7.
levels.prerequisites: Previous level completion

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk part-time (or 2–3 days intensive)
dashboard.core tools: PyTorch, torch.autograd, einops, DataLoader, torch.profiler
dashboard.main project: torch-warmup — a working training loop you can explain
dashboard.final outcome: Build an nn.Module, step an optimiser, and verify checkpoint resume before Level 7.

items.text: Re-do the §1.9 checklist from memory in ten minutes; if any item fails, reread that module before continuing.
`float32` vs `float64` vs `bfloat16`: why the default differs between CPU and GPU, and where a silent downcast changes a result.
`.to(device)` discipline: every tensor in an operation must live on the same device and dtype; know the error message before you meet it.
Views versus copies — `view`, `reshape`, `permute`, `contiguous`, and when `view` throws.
In-place operations and autograd: why `x += 1` can be fine and `x.add_(1)` on a leaf requiring grad is not.
Shape arithmetic with `torch.einsum` and `einops`; write one `einsum` for a batch matmul and check it against `@`.
`nn.Parameter` versus a plain tensor; what `model.parameters()` and `model.named_parameters()` actually yield, and why optimisers receive the former.
`nn.Linear` internals: weight shape `(out, in)`, bias `(out,)`, initialisation distribution.
Composition: `nn.Sequential`, nested modules, and how `state_dict()` flattens names (`0.weight`, `blocks.1.attn.in_proj_weight`).
**Batch dimension first**, always: `(B, F)` in, `(B, C)` out. Most shape bugs in Level 7 are a missing batch axis, not a wrong formula.
Save the `state_dict()`, not the model object; load with `strict=True` and understand what a key mismatch is telling you.
Count parameters by hand for a two-layer MLP, then verify with `sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())`.
The five calls that define training: `optimizer.zero_grad()` → forward → `loss` → `loss.backward()` → `optimizer.step()`. Know what state each one touches.
What actually happens if you forget `zero_grad()`: gradients accumulate across batches, and your effective update silently becomes a sum over history.
Losses: `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` takes **logits**, not probabilities; `BCEWithLogitsLoss` fuses sigmoid and loss for numerical stability; know the `reduction` options.
Optimisers: `SGD` with momentum, `AdamW`; what learning rate does to the first hundred steps; why weight decay is not equivalent to L2 inside adaptive methods.

`model.train()` versus `model.eval()`, and `torch.no_grad()` at inference — the three bugs these prevent: dropout at test time, stale batch-norm statistics, and a retained computation graph that eats memory.
Determinism: `torch.manual_seed`, `np.random.seed`, `random.seed`, DataLoader worker seeding, `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`.
`Dataset` (`__len__`, `__getitem__`) and `DataLoader` (`batch_size`, `shuffle`, `num_workers`, `collate_fn`, `pin_memory`).
Where augmentation belongs (training only) and why an augmentation applied to validation inflates nothing but destroys comparability.
Split discipline: `Subset` with a fixed seed, then assert that no index appears in two splits. This is the Phase 2 leakage rule, re-implemented in framework code.
Throughput: measure samples/sec, then find the bottleneck by comparing `num_workers=0` and `num_workers=8`.

modules.title: Device, precision, and one profiling pass

items.text: Place the model **and** each batch on the same device; then log the device once per run rather than debugging it later.
Mixed precision in ten lines: `torch.autocast` plus `GradScaler`; when the speed-up is not worth the complexity (small models, CPU-only).
Profile one training step with `torch.profiler` and name the top-three time consumers.
Memory: batch size versus activation memory; read `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()` before and after doubling the batch.
Checkpoint the whole run — model, optimiser, epoch, and RNG state — resume it, and verify the loss curve continues rather than jumps.

elements.text: **Acceptance.** Fashion-MNIST reaches ≥ 90% test accuracy in ≤ 3 epochs (MNIST ≥ 97%); a resumed run reproduces the pre-checkpoint loss within $10^{-4}$; loading a saved `state_dict` into a fresh model yields identical logits.

items.text: Write the training loop from a blank file, from memory, five times — deleting it between attempts. Time the fifth; under 15 minutes is the target.

Break the loop four ways on purpose: no `zero_grad()`, loss computed on softmax output, `eval()` left on during training, model on CPU while the batch is on GPU. Record each error message verbatim — you will meet all four again in 7.8.
Predict the parameter count of `nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10))` before running the code; then explain the 2,048-number gap if you used a bias in both layers.
Explain in one paragraph why `step()` must follow `backward()`, and what `backward()` has written into `.grad` by the time `step()` reads it.

elements.text: **Bridge gate.** Do not start 7.1 until every box is ticked. **Rule.** A shaky `optimizer.zero_grad()` costs more time inside 7.4 than this bridge costs now. Treat it as the reference implementation you are about to outgrow: in Level 7 you rebuild this same loop twice, once in NumPy with hand-derived gradients and once in PyTorch with the pieces taken apart.

items.text: `torch-warmup` hits the accuracy target and the checkpoint resume is verified.

levels.title: NEURAL NETWORKS FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES
levels.goal: Build a neural network twice — once in NumPy with hand-derived gradients, once in PyTorch — and understand every line of the training loop. No `model.fit()`, no hidden magic.
levels.prerequisites: Level 2 §2.4 (matrix calculus, chain rule, reverse-mode autograd and gradient checking), Level 4 (a leak-proof feature pipeline), Level 6 (honest splits, intervals, and evaluation discipline), and the **PyTorch readiness bridge** above — Level 1 §1.9 supplies tensors, but `nn.Module`, `torch.optim`, `DataLoader`, and the training loop are taught in that bridge, not in Level 4. Level 4 is a data-and-features level; it is a prerequisite here for pipeline discipline, never for PyTorch.

sections.title: From Classical ML to Neural Networks
sections.objective: Know when a network is the right tool, and what it buys you over a boosted tree.

items.text: Representation learning: features are learned, not hand-built.
Composition of simple non-linear units as a universal approximator.
The three levers: data, compute, and inductive bias.
Regimes where deep learning wins: high-dimensional perceptual data, sequences, generative tasks.
Regimes where it loses: small tabular data, strict interpretability, tight latency with no GPU.
Take a tabular dataset you modelled in L5 and train an MLP on it; report the honest comparison.
Explain, with your numbers, why the GBDT won or lost.
What an inductive bias is, and why it is a *prior*, not a limitation.
MLP: no structure assumed, all connections learned.
CNN: locality and translation equivariance.
RNN: temporal recurrence and weight sharing over time.
Transformer: content-based routing with weak positional prior.
Choosing an architecture is choosing which assumptions are true for your data.
Compute the parameter count of a dense and a convolutional layer with the same input and output width, and explain the ratio.
Write one paragraph on which inductive bias a tabular task violates most.

modules.title: The universal approximation idea, and its limits

items.text: Universal approximation: a wide enough network can approximate a continuous function on a compact set.
Why the theorem says nothing about learnability, data requirements, or generalisation.
Depth versus width: why depth is exponentially more parameter-efficient for some functions.
The gap between "can represent" and "will learn".

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.1).** You can justify using (or not using) a neural network for a specific task with reference to data regime and inductive bias.

Broadcasting rules, and why silent broadcasting is a common bug source.
`view` versus `reshape` versus `permute`; when `.contiguous()` is required.
Indexing, masking, `gather`, `scatter`, and `index_select`.
`einops.rearrange` and `einsum` for readable tensor algebra.
Memory layout and the cost of transposes in hot loops.
Rewrite five `view`/`permute` chains with `einops` and confirm identical outputs.
Reproduce a `view` error caused by a non-contiguous tensor, then fix it correctly.
Write a shape-annotation docstring for every module in a small model.
`nn.Module`: `__init__`, `forward`, submodule registration, and `state_dict`.
Parameters versus buffers: what gets gradients and what gets saved.
`train()` versus `eval()` and the layers that care.
`nn.Sequential`, `nn.ModuleList`, `nn.ModuleDict` and when each is appropriate.
Hooks for inspection: forward hooks, backward hooks, activation statistics.
Freezing and unfreezing parameters.
Build a model with a registered buffer and confirm it moves with `.to(device)`.
Use a forward hook to log activation statistics for every layer in one pass.
Freeze the first half of a network and verify with `requires_grad` and gradient checks.
Nodes as operations, edges as dependencies.
Dynamic graphs in PyTorch versus static graphs in compiled frameworks.
Why the graph is freed after `backward()` and what `retain_graph=True` costs.
Graph breaks and their performance consequence.
Reading a graph visually with `torchviz` or a profiler trace.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.2).** You can trace any shape through a model on paper, and no dimension error surprises you twice.

sections.title: The Perceptron and the MLP
sections.objective: Understand the smallest network completely before scaling up.

items.text: Affine transformation $z=Wx+b$ and its geometric meaning.
Why stacking linear layers collapses to a single linear map.
The role of the activation: introducing curvature.
Feature-space view: a network bends space until classes separate.
Prove algebraically and numerically that a two-layer linear network equals a one-layer linear model.
Visualise how a 2-layer network transforms a 2D dataset before classification.
Sigmoid: saturation and vanishing gradients.
Tanh: zero-centred but still saturating.
ReLU: cheap, sparse, and the dying-ReLU failure mode.
Leaky ReLU, ELU, GELU, SiLU: what each fixes.
Choosing an activation: modern defaults and why they changed.
Train identical networks with sigmoid versus ReLU and plot gradient norms per layer.
Create dying ReLUs with a large learning rate and demonstrate the fix.
Binary: one logit with `BCEWithLogitsLoss` (never sigmoid + BCELoss).
Multiclass: logits with `CrossEntropyLoss`, which applies log-softmax internally.
Regression: linear output with MSE, L1, or Huber.
Counts: Poisson or negative-binomial output parameterisation.
Why passing probabilities where logits are expected is a silent quality bug.
Show numerically that sigmoid + BCE produces worse gradients than BCE-with-logits at extreme logits.
Implement `CrossEntropyLoss` from logits and verify against PyTorch.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.3).** You can choose the correct output layer and loss for five task types, and explain the failure mode of each wrong choice.

sections.title: Backpropagation from Scratch
sections.objective: Derive and implement the backward pass yourself, for a network with multiple layers.

modules.title: The chain rule on the graph

items.text: Forward pass: cache the intermediate values you will need.
Backward pass: start from $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathcal{L}=1$ and walk the graph in reverse topological order.
The three reusable local gradients: linear, activation, loss.
Shape discipline: every gradient has the shape of the thing it differentiates.
Derive the backward pass for a 3-layer MLP with ReLU and softmax cross-entropy, on paper.
Implement it in NumPy, then verify every parameter's gradient with finite differences.
Layer classes with `forward` returning output plus cache, and `backward` consuming an upstream gradient.
A `Sequential` container that chains forward and reverse.
Loss modules with their own backward.
An optimiser that consumes gradients and updates parameters.
A training loop with batching, shuffling, and epoch-level validation.
Implement a 2-layer MLP on MNIST in NumPy, reaching at least 96% test accuracy.
Implement momentum and compare convergence against plain SGD at the same learning rate.
Central differences and the choice of epsilon.
Relative error thresholds and why absolute thresholds mislead.
Checking a random subset of parameters rather than all of them.
Common gradient bugs: missing transpose, wrong axis in a sum, forgetting the bias gradient, double-counting a shared parameter.
Write a `grad_check` utility that reports per-parameter relative error.
Deliberately break the transpose in the linear layer and confirm the checker catches it.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.4).** Your NumPy MLP trains on MNIST with gradient-checked layers, and you can teach the backward pass on a whiteboard without notes.

sections.title: Automatic Differentiation
sections.objective: Understand the machinery that replaces your hand-written backward pass.

items.text: Each tensor carries `grad_fn` and `requires_grad`.
Reverse-mode differentiation over a dynamically built graph.
Leaf tensors accumulate gradients; non-leaf tensors free them.
`torch.no_grad()` for inference and evaluation, and its memory effect.
`detach()` versus `.data` — and why `detach` is the correct habit.

elements.latex: \text{var}(x)\ \text{for } x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) \Rightarrow \text{grad accumulates across backward calls unless zeroed}

items.text: Print `grad_fn` chains for three expressions and draw the corresponding graph.
Reproduce gradient accumulation by omitting `zero_grad()` and explain the numbers.
Subclassing `torch.autograd.Function` with `forward` and `backward`.
Saving tensors for backward with `ctx.save_for_backward`.
Marking non-differentiable outputs.
When a custom function is worth writing (memory, numerics, a fused kernel).
Implement a stable log-sum-exp as a custom autograd function and gradient-check it.
Implement a straight-through estimator for quantisation and verify gradients flow.
Registering backward hooks to capture per-layer gradient norms.
Detecting vanishing and exploding gradients early.
Gradient clipping as a diagnostic *and* a fix.
The gradient/parameter norm ratio as a training-health signal.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.5).** You can explain why autograd exists, write one custom function, and diagnose a training run from gradient statistics alone.

sections.title: Initialisation and Signal Propagation
sections.objective: Start training from a point where gradients can actually flow.

items.text: Zero initialisation: all units identical, no symmetry breaking.
Constant initialisation: same problem, different constant.
Too large: saturated activations and exploding forward pass.
Too small: shrinking signal and vanishing gradients.
The variance-preservation goal: keep activation variance constant across layers.
Train with three initialisation scales and plot activation variance per layer.
Show that symmetry prevents a zero-initialised network from learning.
Xavier/Glorot for tanh and linear activations.
He/Kaiming for ReLU (factor of 2 for the rectifier's variance).
Orthogonal initialisation for recurrent and deep stacks.
Bias initialisation, and why a small positive bias helps ReLU.
Initialisation for residual networks: scaling the residual branch.
Compare Xavier and He on a 20-layer ReLU network; report the depth at which each fails.
Show that orthogonal initialisation improves an LSTM's early training stability.

modules.title: Normalisation at the point of initialisation

items.text: Why normalisation layers reduce initialisation sensitivity.
Pre-norm residuals and their effect on gradient flow.
The interaction between initialisation scale and learning rate.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.6).** Given a failing deep network, you can identify whether the problem is initialisation, normalisation, or learning rate — and fix it.

sections.title: Data Loading and the Training Loop
sections.objective: Make the loop correct and fast, because a slow or wrong loop wastes weeks.

items.text: `Dataset` protocol: `__len__` and `__getitem__`.
Batching, shuffling, `drop_last`, and deterministic worker seeding.
`num_workers`, pinning memory, and where the bottleneck usually is.
Collation for variable-length sequences (padding and masking).
Custom samplers: stratified, weighted, curriculum, and distributed.
Build a dataset that loads images from disk and measure throughput at 0, 2, 4 workers.
Show the training loop starved by the data loader, then fix it.
Zero gradients, forward, loss, backward, step — in that order.
Train versus eval mode, and `torch.no_grad()` for validation.
Metric accumulation across batches without holding tensors.
Checkpointing: model, optimiser, scheduler, epoch, and RNG state.
Resuming training and proving it is bit-comparable.
Write the loop from memory, with checkpointing and resume.
Kill a run mid-epoch, resume it, and confirm the loss curve is continuous.

modules.title: Overfit one batch as the first test

items.text: Why memorising ten examples isolates optimisation from generalisation.
Interpreting success and failure of the overfit test.
Common causes of failure: label mismatch, wrong loss, frozen parameters, detached graph, learning rate.
The second test: verify the loss at initialisation is near $\log K$ for $K$ classes.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.7).** You can write the loop from memory and diagnose a model that fails the one-batch test in under ten minutes.

sections.title: Regularisation for Neural Networks
sections.objective: Control capacity deliberately, not by adding dropout everywhere and hoping.

items.text: Dropout: masking, scaling, and the train/eval difference.
Why dropout at inference must be disabled (and the calibration damage if it is not).
Inverted dropout and the $1/(1-p)$ rescaling.
Dropout on embeddings, attention, and residual branches.
Variants: spatial dropout, DropPath/stochastic depth, and when each is used.
Show accuracy collapsing when eval mode forgets to disable dropout.
Compare dropout rates 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 on the same architecture with a fixed protocol.

modules.title: Weight decay, early stopping and augmentation

items.text: $L_2$ regularisation versus decoupled weight decay (AdamW).
Early stopping on a validation metric, with patience and min-delta.
Data augmentation as the strongest regulariser for vision and audio.
Label smoothing and its effect on calibration.
Mixup, CutMix, and their interaction with small datasets.
Compare Adam with $L_2$ in the loss versus AdamW on the same task.
Show early stopping preventing overfitting and report the epoch it fires.
Diagnose first: is the gap between train and validation large, or is both high?
Regularise the side that is failing.
Budget-aware choices: augmentation costs compute, dropout costs nothing.
Interactions: dropout plus weight decay plus augmentation is not automatically better.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.8).** Each regulariser in your model has a measured justification and a known cost.

sections.title: Debugging Neural Networks
sections.objective: Turn "it doesn't learn" into a specific, testable hypothesis within minutes.

elements.text: Run these in order, and never skip a rung:

items.text: **Can it overfit ten examples?** If not, the bug is in the model, loss, labels, or gradient path.
**Is the initial loss sensible?** For $K$ classes, expect about $\log K$.
**Are shapes and dtypes what you think?** Print once with labels, not everywhere.
**Are gradients flowing?** Check per-layer gradient norms, not just the total.
**Is the data what you think it is?** Visualise inputs, labels, and a few predictions.
**Is the learning rate sane?** A five-point log sweep costs minutes and answers everything.
**Only then** consider architecture and regularisation.
Take five broken training scripts and diagnose each using only the ladder.
Record which rung found the bug and how long it took.
Train falling, validation falling: healthy.
Train falling, validation rising: overfitting.
Both flat and high: underfitting or a broken gradient.
Both high and unstable: learning rate too high or data problem.
Sudden spikes: bad batch, exploding gradients, or a data pipeline fault.
Periodic oscillation: batch-size or sampler interaction.
Generate synthetic loss curves for each failure mode and write the correct diagnosis and intervention for each.
Match six real (anonymised) curve screenshots to their causes.

rows: Dead units after a few steps

sections.title: Mini-project: Break and fix a training loop

modules.title: Mini-project: Break and fix a training loop

items.text: Take a working MNIST classifier.

Introduce **eight deliberate faults**: wrong loss for logits, frozen first layer, missing `zero_grad`, dropout left on at eval, learning rate 100× too high, labels shuffled, `detach()` in the middle of the graph, and a data loader that returns the same batch every step.
For each fault: write the symptom, the diagnostic that identifies it, the fix, and the test that would catch it next time.

items.text: Convex versus non-convex: what guarantees are lost.
Local minima, plateaus, and saddle points; why saddles dominate in high dimensions.

The empirical finding: many well-performing low-loss regions, connected by paths.
Why convergence theory for convex optimisation does not transfer directly.

\Pr(\text{all positive})\to 0\ \text{as }d\to\infty

subBlocks.title: Project: `dynamics-lab` — an optimisation and stability study

levels.title: DEEP LEARNING ARCHITECTURES
levels.goal: Learn the major architecture families well enough to choose one from evidence: convolutions, recurrence, attention, and generative designs. Then make them cheap enough to ship.
levels.prerequisites: Level 8. You must be able to train stably before you can fairly compare architectures.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: PyTorch, `torchvision`, `timm`, `einops`, Hugging Face `transformers`, `torch.profiler`
dashboard.main project: **`arch-zoo`** — five architectures, one task, one controlled comparison

sections.title: Architectural Thinking
sections.objective: Choose an architecture by reasoning about the data, not by copying the state of the art.

modules.title: The four questions before any architecture choice

items.text: What is the structure of the input? (grid, sequence, set, graph, tabular)
Which invariances are true? (translation, permutation, time order)

What are the latency, memory, and data budgets?
Matching inductive bias to data structure.

subBlocks.title: Project: `arch-zoo` — five architectures, one task, one honest comparison

elements.text: **Purpose.** Build the comparison that lets you say, with evidence, which architecture you would ship and why. This is the single most useful artefact for deep-learning interviews.

items.text: One dataset you can train five models on within your compute budget (CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, a text classification set, or a small audio set).
A fixed evaluation protocol from Level 6, committed before experiments.
An MLP baseline (from Level 7).
A CNN (ResNet-style, from scratch).
A pretrained CNN fine-tuned.
A transformer (ViT-style or text transformer, from scratch or pretrained).
One architecture of your choice: RNN/LSTM, a small GNN, or a compact diffusion model if your task is generative.
Equal-parameter and equal-FLOP comparisons for at least two pairs.
Learning rate tuned per architecture (range test each).
Three seeds minimum per architecture.
Report accuracy, macro-F1, latency at p50/p95, parameters, FLOPs, and peak memory.
Compress the best model with quantisation, pruning, or distillation.
Report the accuracy/size/latency trade-off against the uncompressed baseline.
A model card for the winning model.
A one-page recommendation memo with the rejected architectures and reasons.

arch-zoo/
├── conf/
│   ├── protocol.yaml       # frozen before experiments
│   └── models/*.yaml
├── src/arch_zoo/
│   ├── data.py
│   ├── models/
│   │   ├── mlp.py
│   │   ├── cnn.py
│   │   ├── vit.py
│   │   ├── rnn.py
│   │   └── registry.py     # name → constructor, params, FLOPs
│   ├── train.py
│   ├── compare.py          # matched-budget comparison tables
│   ├── compress.py         # quantise, prune, distil
│   ├── benchmark.py        # latency percentiles, memory
│   └── card.py             # model card generator
├── reports/
│   ├── comparison.md
│   ├── efficiency.md
│   ├── model_card.md
│   └── recommendation.md
└── tests/

rows: Committed before experiments; identical eval set for all models
LR tuned per model; equal-parameter and equal-FLOP tables
Parameters, FLOPs, p50/p95 latency, peak memory for every model
At least one method applied to the winner, with measured trade-off
Model card and recommendation memo complete
One command regenerates every table and figure

Implement one architecture from its paper, not from a library.
Add a scaling study: three sizes of the winning family.
Serve the compressed model behind an API and load-test it.
Compare against a strong tabular baseline if your task permits.

elements.text: Level 9 is complete when you can defend your architecture choice against a cheaper and a stronger alternative, with numbers from your own runs.

elements.text: **Level 9 completion rule.** If you can pick an architecture from constraints, train it stably, compress it to a budget, and defend the choice with your own numbers — you are ready for Phase 4.

levels.title: REPRESENTATION AND SELF-SUPERVISED LEARNING
levels.goal: Understand how models learn useful features without labels, how to train such models on a modest budget, and how to prove the representation is actually good — with a frozen probe, not with vibes.
levels.prerequisites: Level 9 (architectures), Level 8 (training dynamics), Level 6 (evaluation protocol).

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: PyTorch, `timm`, `torchvision`, `faiss`, `scikit-learn` (probes), `umap-learn`
dashboard.main project: **`repr-lab`** — pretrain a small encoder with SSL, evaluate it frozen, and ablate the design
dashboard.final outcome: Train a self-supervised encoder, evaluate it without fine-tuning, detect collapse, and explain which design choice mattered.

sections.title: What a Representation Is
sections.objective: Define the object you are optimising, and how you will know it is good.

items.text: A representation as a map $f_\theta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^d$.
What good representations share: smoothness, disentanglement, invariance to nuisance, linear separability of factors.
Dimensionality, capacity, and the information bottleneck intuition.
Embedding geometry: cosine versus Euclidean, norm concentration, hubness.
Why the same encoder can be excellent for retrieval and useless for classification.
Train an autoencoder and inspect its latent space with PCA and UMAP.
Show two downstream tasks where the same representation ranks differently in quality.

modules.title: The three ways to obtain a representation

items.text: Supervised learning as representation learning (labels shape the features).
Self-supervised learning: build the pretext task from the data itself.
Transfer from a pretrained foundation model.
Trade-offs: label cost, compute cost, task specificity, and control.
Why SSL matters: unlabelled data is abundant, labels are not.
For three problems, decide between supervised, SSL, and pretrained transfer, with a cost estimate.
Quantify how many labels a supervised model needs to match a frozen pretrained encoder on your task.

modules.title: Evaluating representations before you build them

items.text: Linear probe: freeze the encoder, train a linear classifier on labels.
k-NN evaluation: no training at all, purely geometric.
Fine-tuning as the upper bound, not the primary metric.
Transfer across datasets and label fractions.
Clustering quality and nearest-neighbour visual inspection.
Evaluate one encoder with linear probe, k-NN, and fine-tuning; explain the gaps.
Show a probe ranking that reverses when label fraction is reduced to 1%.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.1).** You can evaluate any encoder with a frozen probe and k-NN, and explain what each measures.

sections.title: Contrastive Learning
sections.objective: Learn invariance by pulling positives together and pushing negatives apart.

items.text: Positive pairs from augmentations; negatives from other examples in the batch.
Temperature and its effect on the softness of the distribution.
Why this is a lower bound on mutual information (intuition, not proof).
The alignment–uniformity trade-off.
Batch size and the number of negatives.
Implement InfoNCE and verify it decreases as positive similarity rises.
Sweep $\tau\in\{0.05,0.1,0.5\}$ and describe the effect on the embedding geometry.
The projection head and why representations are taken *before* it.
Augmentation composition: crop, colour jitter, blur, flip.
Large batches and the memory cost of many negatives.
Why strong augmentation is the main driver of quality.
The linear-probe protocol as the standard evaluation.
Run an augmentation ablation: remove colour jitter, then cropping, and measure probe accuracy.
Show that removing the projection head hurts the linear probe.
The momentum encoder and the queue of negatives.
Why a queue decouples batch size from the number of negatives.
Momentum coefficient and the stability of the key encoder.
BYOL-style asymmetry and the collapse question.
Practical trade-offs: memory, complexity, and result quality.
Train MoCo-style with a small batch and compare against SimCLR at equal compute.
Show the queue's negative count versus probe accuracy curve.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.2).** You have trained a contrastive encoder and can point to the augmentation and temperature choices that mattered.

sections.title: Masked and Predictive Modelling
sections.objective: Learn representations by reconstruction or prediction rather than comparison.

items.text: Masking strategies: random token, span, structured patches.
Mask ratio and the information–difficulty trade-off.
Encoder-only masked modelling (BERT) versus decoder reconstruction (MAE).
Why MAE needs a high mask ratio in vision but BERT does not in text.
The evaluation protocol: probe, fine-tune, or generate.
Train a small masked autoencoder and probe it against a contrastive baseline at equal compute.
Sweep mask ratio 25%, 50%, 75% and report probe accuracy.
Next-token prediction as self-supervision.
Why language modelling scales well and what it optimises implicitly.
The difference between learning to predict and learning to represent.
Prefix/suffix prediction and other variants.
When to use generative pretraining versus contrastive pretraining.
Train a tiny causal model on a text corpus and probe its hidden states for sentiment.
Compare a causal and a masked objective on the same corpus and task.
Plain autoencoders versus denoising autoencoders.
Why reconstruction often produces features that are worse for classification.
Bottleneck design and what it forces.
When reconstruction is exactly the right objective (compression, anomaly detection).

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.3).** You can choose between contrastive, masked, and generative pretraining with reasons, and run the comparison yourself.

sections.title: Non-Contrastive and Redundancy-Reduction Methods
sections.objective: Understand the families that avoid negatives, and why they do not collapse.

items.text: Online and target networks; predictor heads and stop-gradients.
Why collapse does not happen in practice (hypotheses, not proofs).
EMA teacher and centring in DINO.
Hyperparameter sensitivity: these methods are famously finicky.
Practical recommendation: use a well-tested recipe before inventing your own.
Train BYOL on a small dataset and check for collapse by measuring embedding variance.
Remove the stop-gradient and reproduce collapse; document what happens.
Cross-correlation matrix and the goal of identity.
Invariance and redundancy terms as explicit objectives.
Why these methods need no negatives, no predictor, and no EMA.
Their sensitivity to batch size and augmentation strength.
When explicit variance terms make debugging easier.
Implement both terms and verify that the off-diagonal penalty drives cross-correlation to zero.
Compare Barlow Twins and SimCLR at equal batch size on a small dataset.
Complete collapse: all outputs identical, zero variance.
Dimensional collapse: effective rank far below $d$.
Diagnostics: singular-value spectrum of the embedding matrix, entropy of the similarity distribution.
Fixes: variance terms, stop-gradients, centring, whitening.
Reporting effective rank as a standard metric.
Measure effective rank for a healthy and a collapsed run and plot the spectra.
Break a working method deliberately and identify collapse from the diagnostics.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.4).** You can explain why a negative-free method does not collapse, and prove with diagnostics that your run did not.

sections.title: Multimodal and Cross-Modal Representations
sections.objective: Align representations across modalities and use them for zero-shot transfer.

items.text: Paired image–text data and the dual-encoder architecture.
Symmetric InfoNCE over the batch, with a learned temperature.
Zero-shot classification via prompt templates.
What alignment buys: retrieval, captioning support, and weak supervision.
Failure modes: compositional reasoning, counting, and fine-grained spatial relations.
Use a pretrained CLIP model for zero-shot classification and compare with a supervised baseline.
Show one task where prompt wording changes accuracy by more than five points.
Early fusion, late fusion, and cross-attention.
Audio–text and video–text alignment.
Modality gaps and missing-modality robustness.
Evaluating cross-modal retrieval with recall@k and mean rank.
Data quality: noisy pairs and their effect on alignment.
Evaluate a cross-modal retrieval model and inspect the false positives.
Add synthetic noise to pairs and measure the degradation in recall@10.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.5).** You can use a multimodal encoder for zero-shot transfer and explain where alignment breaks.

sections.title: Transfer, Probing and Adaptation Protocols
sections.objective: Compare representations fairly, which is harder than it sounds.

items.text: Frozen encoder plus linear probe: the standard.
k-NN evaluation: parameter-free, sensitive to normalisation.
Fine-tuning with a conservative learning rate; layer-wise decay.
Partial unfreezing and adapter-based adaptation.
Label-efficiency curves: accuracy versus fraction of labels.
Same probe protocol for every encoder, same augmentation, same epochs.
Reporting compute spent to obtain the representation, not only the probe score.
Build a probe harness that evaluates three encoders with identical settings and reports intervals.
Show that a probe can rank encoders differently at 1%, 10%, and 100% of labels.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.6).** Every representation comparison you report uses one frozen protocol and includes compute cost.

sections.title: Representation Quality and Failure Modes
sections.objective: Understand what SSL encoders actually learn, including the shortcuts.

items.text: Shortcut learning: background, texture, colour, and dataset artefacts.
Augmentation leakage: an augmentation that destroys the signal you need downstream.
Negative sampling bias in contrastive learning.
Spurious correlations that survive pretraining and poison downstream tasks.
Domain shift: a representation tuned to ImageNet may not transfer to microscopy.
Feature attribution and nearest-neighbour inspection as diagnostics.
Reporting: probe accuracy is necessary but not sufficient — inspect the neighbours.
Find a case where a high-probe encoder has visibly wrong nearest neighbours.
Show that colour-only augmentation destroys performance on a colour-relevant task.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.7).** You can name the shortcut your encoder learned and show evidence for it.

sections.title: Metric Learning and Embedding Systems
sections.objective: Learn embeddings for a specific distance-based task, which is most of industry retrieval.

items.text: Triplet loss, margin selection, and hard-negative mining.
Contrastive and margin-based losses (ArcFace, CosFace) for classification embeddings.
Sampling strategies: batch-hard, semi-hard, and curriculum.
Evaluation with recall@k, precision@k, and mAP.
Embedding dimensionality versus retrieval cost.
Indexing for retrieval: FAISS, IVF, HNSW, and quantisation.
When to learn embeddings versus when to use a pretrained model frozen.
Train a metric-learning model on a small fine-grained dataset; report recall@1 and recall@10.
Compare no mining, random mining, and hard mining on the same budget.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.8).** You can train, evaluate, and index an embedding model for a retrieval task.

sections.title: Critiques and Limits of SSL
sections.objective: Know the arguments against the field's claims, so you do not repeat them uncritically.

items.text: "SSL removes the need for labels" — until you need a task-specific decision boundary.
Compute cost: pretraining is expensive, and the savings only appear at scale.
Benchmark dependence: many gains are ImageNet-shaped.
Reproducibility problems: sensitive recipes, unreported compute.
Evaluation leakage: probing on data the encoder may have seen.
Interpretability: latent spaces are harder to audit than hand-built features.
When a supervised or classical approach still wins in practice.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.9).** You can argue both for and against using SSL for a given problem, with costs.

items.text: Implement the InfoNCE loss from scratch, with temperature.
Build a two-view augmentation pipeline with configurable transforms.
Train a small CNN on CIFAR-10 with SimCLR for a fixed budget.
Evaluate with a frozen linear probe and k-NN.
Run three ablations: augmentation set, temperature, projection-head depth.
Report probe accuracy with intervals, effective rank, and compute used.

elements.text: **Gate.** Your probe beats a randomly initialised encoder by a wide margin, the ablations identify the key design choice, and you can explain the loss line by line.
**Purpose.** Produce a rigorous representation-learning study. This is the artefact that demonstrates you understand modern pretraining rather than simply calling a pretrained model.

items.text: At least two SSL objectives implemented or adapted: one contrastive (SimCLR or MoCo) and one non-contrastive (BYOL or Barlow Twins).
Configurable augmentation pipeline with named presets.
Checkpointing, resumption, and run metadata logging.
Collapse diagnostics logged every epoch: embedding variance, effective rank, similarity histogram.
Linear probe and k-NN for every checkpoint.
Label-efficiency curves at 1%, 10%, and 100% of labels.
Probe protocol identical across encoders, with three seeds and intervals.
Comparison against a supervised baseline trained on the same budget.
Objective: contrastive versus non-contrastive versus supervised versus random init.
Augmentation: full set, minus crops, minus colour, crops only.
Temperature or EMA momentum, whichever applies.
Batch size at fixed compute.
t-SNE or UMAP of the embedding space, before and after pretraining.
Nearest-neighbour inspections for 20 samples, with commentary on correctness.
One documented failure: a shortcut learned, an augmentation that hurt, or a collapse that occurred.
A results table with probe accuracy, k-NN accuracy, effective rank, and compute for every configuration.
A one-page conclusion: which design choice mattered most, and why.
Reproduction instructions that rebuild every number.

Probe accuracy lift of at least 15 points on CIFAR-10-scale data
Honest comparison at matched compute, with the gap stated

At least 8 configurations, one variable each
One concrete shortcut or failure documented with evidence

items.text: Add MoCo-style momentum encoder and compare queue-based negatives with in-batch negatives.
Pretrain on unlabelled data from your own domain and transfer to a labelled subset.
Add a multimodal alignment experiment with image–text pairs you assemble.
Distil the pretrained encoder into a much smaller one and measure the quality retained.
Evaluate transfer to two downstream datasets instead of one.

Frozen probe for every comparison, three seeds, intervals
Collapse metrics logged and interpreted, not just collected
