elements.text: Level 10 is complete when you can defend the claim "this representation is better" with a frozen probe, seed variance, and a stated compute budget.

questions.question: What makes a representation good?
Why can two encoders rank differently for retrieval and classification?
What is a linear probe, and what does it measure?
Why is k-NN evaluation useful, and what is its weakness?
What is a shortcut feature, and how do you detect one?
Explain InfoNCE and the role of temperature.
Why do negatives matter, and what happens with too few?
Why is the projection head discarded after pretraining?
Why does augmenting strongly help SimCLR?
How does MoCo decouple batch size from the number of negatives?
Why doesn't BYOL collapse?
What does the stop-gradient do?
How do Barlow Twins and VICReg enforce non-collapse?
What is dimensional collapse, and how do you measure it?
How does CLIP's objective work, and what does it enable?
Where does CLIP fail, and why?
Explain triplet loss and hard-negative mining.
How do you evaluate an embedding model for retrieval?
What are the strongest arguments against current SSL claims?
When would you use SSL instead of supervised learning, and when not?
Your SSL encoder has high probe accuracy but bad nearest neighbours. What now?
How would you pretrain on 50k unlabelled images from your domain with one GPU?

items.text: I can define and evaluate a representation with frozen probes.
I can implement InfoNCE and explain temperature.
I can explain SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, and Barlow Twins.
I can describe masked and generative pretraining objectives.
I can use multimodal encoders for zero-shot transfer.
I can train metric-learning embeddings and index them.
I can detect collapse and shortcut learning.
I can state the honest costs and limits of SSL.
I have pretrained an encoder with two different objectives.
I have evaluated with linear probe and k-NN at multiple label fractions.
I have run ablation studies with seed variance.
I have measured effective rank and inspected nearest neighbours.
I have documented one real failure with evidence.
`repr-lab` passes every acceptance target.
The results table includes compute for every configuration.
I can defend the claim "this representation is better" under scrutiny.

elements.text: **Level 10 completion rule.** If you can pretrain, probe, and critique a representation model with your own numbers, you are ready for Level 11.

levels.title: ADVANCED ML METHODS
levels.goal: Add the methods that a senior applied scientist is expected to know but that Phase 2 does not cover: uncertainty, causality, sequences, recommendation, adaptation under shift, and constrained optimisation. You will implement two of them deeply rather than skim ten.
levels.prerequisites: Levels 5–9. These methods assume honest evaluation, solid modelling, and the ability to train and debug networks.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: PyTorch, `statsmodels`, `EconML`/`DoWhy`, `sktime`/`statsforecast`, `scikit-learn`, `PyMC` or `numpyro` (optional)
dashboard.main project: **`adv-ml-lab`** — two advanced methods implemented, benchmarked, and reported
dashboard.final outcome: Select and correctly apply advanced methods, state their assumptions, and measure whether they beat simpler alternatives.

sections.title: Uncertainty Quantification
sections.objective: Produce predictions that know what they do not know.

items.text: Aleatoric: irreducible noise in the data.
Epistemic: uncertainty about the model, reducible with more data.
Why the distinction changes the decision (collect data versus accept the noise).
Calibration versus uncertainty: related but not identical.
Out-of-distribution inputs as a separate failure mode.
Estimate total, aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainty on a synthetic dataset with known noise.
Show that adding training data reduces the epistemic term but not the aleatoric one.
Deep ensembles: train $k$ models and treat the spread as uncertainty.
MC dropout: dropout at inference, multiple stochastic passes.
Snapshot ensembles and their cheaper cost.
Quantile regression and distributional heads.
Conformal prediction as a distribution-free wrapper (from L6).
Cost comparison: ensembles multiply training and inference cost.
Compare deep ensembles, MC dropout, and conformal intervals on coverage and cost.
Show MC dropout underestimating uncertainty on OOD inputs relative to ensembles.
Priors, posteriors, and why full Bayesian inference is expensive.
Variational inference and the ELBO (from Level 9).
Laplace approximation as a post-hoc method.
Bayesian neural networks: when they are worth the complexity.
Decision-theoretic use: expected loss minimisation under uncertainty.
Honest recommendation: most problems need calibration and ensembles, not a posterior.
Implement a Laplace approximation on a small trained network and compare intervals with an ensemble.
Write a decision rule that uses predictive uncertainty to route low-confidence cases to humans.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.1).** You can produce calibrated, uncertainty-aware predictions and justify the method's cost.

sections.title: Kernel and Gaussian Process Methods
sections.objective: Know when a principled non-parametric model beats a deep net.

items.text: Kernel functions and the feature-space view.
Gaussian processes: mean and covariance functions, posterior predictive.
Hyperparameter learning by marginal likelihood.
Computational cost $O(n^3)$ and the approximations: inducing points, random features, Nyström.
Multi-output and structured kernels.
Where GPs win: small data, smooth functions, well-calibrated uncertainty, active learning.
Where they lose: scale, high dimensions, non-stationary data.
Fit a GP regression with a squared-exponential kernel and compare intervals with a neural network.
Use a GP for Bayesian optimisation of two hyperparameters.
Show GP failure at $n=10^5$ without approximation and fix it with inducing points.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.2).** You can choose a GP for a stated problem and explain its cost.

sections.title: Sequence, Time Series and Forecasting
sections.objective: Forecast and model sequential data without the classic validation mistakes.

items.text: Trend, seasonality, and residual decomposition.
Naive, seasonal-naive, and moving-average baselines (always the baseline).
Exponential smoothing and ARIMA families.
Cross-validation for time series: rolling origin with a horizon gap.
Metrics that matter: MASE, sMAPE, pinball loss for quantiles.
Forecast a public series with three baselines and one ARIMA model; report MASE with intervals.
Show a random split inflating forecast accuracy and fix it with rolling origin.
Local versus global models; why one model across many series often wins.
Gradient-boosted forecasting with lag and calendar features.
Deep forecasters: DeepAR, N-BEATS, TFT, and simple LSTMs.
Hierarchical forecasting and reconciliation.
Intermittent and sparse demand.
Probabilistic forecasting with quantile or distributional heads.
Build a global LightGBM forecaster and compare it with per-series models.
Produce 80% and 95% prediction intervals and measure their empirical coverage.
Sequence classification and event prediction with irregular sampling.
Survival analysis: censoring, Kaplan–Meier, Cox models, and deep survival.
Churn and time-to-event problems framed correctly.
Dynamic treatment and sequential decisions (preview of 11.5).
Frame a churn problem as survival analysis and compare with binary classification at a fixed horizon.
Show how censoring biases a naive classification target.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.3).** You can forecast, validate temporally, and produce calibrated prediction intervals.

sections.title: Causal Machine Learning
sections.objective: Estimate effects, not just correlations, and know exactly when you cannot.

items.text: Potential outcomes and the estimands: ATE, ATT, CATE.
Confounding, backdoor paths, and adjustment sets.
DAGs as a reasoning tool.
Instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, and difference-in-differences.
Sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding.
Draw a DAG for a product question and derive the minimal adjustment set.
Simulate a confounded dataset and show naive estimation is biased while adjusted estimation is not.
Meta-learners: S-learner, T-learner, X-learner.
Doubly robust estimation and double machine learning.
Causal forests for heterogeneous effects.
Uplift modelling and its evaluation.
Overlap and positivity: where causal estimates are unsupported.
Why predictive accuracy is irrelevant to causal validity.

elements.latex:
\hat\tau_{\text{AIPW}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\left[\frac{T_iY_i}{\hat e(X_i)}-\frac{(1-T_i)Y_i}{1-\hat e(X_i)}\right]
-\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\frac{T_i-\hat e(X_i)}{\hat e(X_i)\left(1-\hat e(X_i)\right)}\hat m(X_i)

items.text: Estimate a treatment effect with a meta-learner and with double ML on simulated data; compare with the truth.
Measure overlap and identify the region where the effect is unidentified.
Evaluating CATE estimators without ground truth: simulation, proxy metrics, and calibration of uplift.
Qini and uplift curves.
The failure mode: a great uplift model on a bad identification strategy.
Reporting causal results: estimand, assumption, estimator, interval, sensitivity.
Compare two uplift models with Qini curves and pick an operating point.
Write a one-page causal report with all five reporting elements.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.4).** You can state an estimand, defend the identification assumption, and report an effect with uncertainty and sensitivity.

sections.title: Sequential Decision Making and Bandits
sections.objective: Optimise decisions over time without wrecking the product.

items.text: Exploration versus exploitation; regret.
Multi-armed bandits: epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling.
Contextual bandits and their relationship to recommendation.
Off-policy evaluation: inverse propensity scoring, doubly robust, and their assumptions.
Logging policies and the data you must record to evaluate offline.
Switching from A/B testing to bandits: when it is legitimate and when it is risky.
Guardrails, delayed feedback, and the cost of exploration.
Simulate a three-arm bandit with all three policies and plot cumulative regret.
Run off-policy evaluation on a logged dataset and show IPS blowing up when propensities are tiny.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.5).** You can design a bandit experiment, log it correctly, and evaluate it offline.

sections.title: Recommenders and Ranking
sections.objective: Build and evaluate systems whose output is an ordered list.

items.text: Candidate generation, ranking, and re-ranking as separate stages.
Implicit versus explicit feedback.
Matrix factorisation, BPR, and two-tower retrieval models.
Learning to rank: pointwise, pairwise, listwise; LambdaMART.
Sequential recommenders and session-based models.
Position bias, exposure bias, and click models.
Evaluation: recall@k, nDCG, MAP, plus diversity, coverage, and novelty.
Cold start and the exploration problem.
Build a two-tower retriever plus a ranking model; report recall@50 for retrieval and nDCG@10 for ranking.
Show how position bias inflates the apparent quality of top-ranked items.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.6).** You can build a two-stage recommender and evaluate each stage with the right metric.

sections.title: Distribution Shift, Robustness and Adaptation
sections.objective: Handle the fact that production data is not your test set.

items.text: Covariate shift: $P(X)$ changes, $P(y\mid X)$ stable.
Label shift: $P(y)$ changes.
Concept drift: $P(y\mid X)$ changes.
Domain shift and subpopulation shift.
Adversarial and corrupted inputs.
Detecting shift: statistical tests, drift scores, and proxy signals.
Simulate each shift type on one dataset and measure the metric degradation.
Detect covariate shift with a domain classifier and quantify separability.
Importance weighting and its variance problem.
Domain adaptation: feature alignment, adversarial alignment, and pseudo-labelling.
Domain generalisation: augmentation, invariance penalties, and their limits.
Test-time adaptation and continual learning basics.
Group distributionally robust optimisation.
Adversarial training and its cost.
Apply importance weighting under covariate shift and compare with naive training.
Show adversarial training reducing robustness-cost trade-offs on a clean accuracy curve.
Confidence-based baselines: max softmax, entropy.
Distance-based methods: Mahalanobis, k-NN, energy scores.
Models with explicit density estimates.
Evaluation: AUROC, AUPR, and the effect of the OOD set you chose.
Why OOD detection results rarely transfer across benchmarks.
Compare three OOD detectors across two OOD datasets and show rankings changing.
Calibrate an abstention rule using OOD scores and measure the human-review load.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.7).** You can name the shift your system faces, measure it, and choose a mitigation with a stated cost.

sections.title: Anomaly Detection and Rare Events
sections.objective: Work where positives are scarce and expensive.

items.text: Framings: supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised.
Reconstruction-based detection and its assumptions.
One-class methods and density estimation.
Extreme value theory for threshold setting.
Alert budget and precision at a fixed alert rate.
Evaluation without labels: injection studies and expert review.
Human-in-the-loop design and feedback capture.
Inject 200 known anomalies into clean data and measure detection at 100 alerts per day.
Show a detector with high AUROC and unusable precision at the operating threshold.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.8).** You can design an anomaly system around an alert budget and evaluate it honestly.

sections.title: Multi-Objective and Constrained Optimisation
sections.objective: Optimise for accuracy **and** latency, cost, fairness, or safety.

items.text: Multi-objective optimisation and the Pareto frontier.
Scalarisation, and why it hides trade-offs.
Constrained optimisation: Lagrangian relaxation, and projected methods.
Cost-sensitive learning and budgeted decisions.
Fairness-accuracy trade-offs and their measurement.
Reporting a frontier instead of a single model.
Choosing an operating point with stakeholders.
Sweep a model size and plot accuracy versus latency as a Pareto frontier.
Implement a simple Lagrangian constraint on inference cost and show the frontier shift.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.9).** You present trade-offs as frontiers and can defend an operating point.

sections.title: Choosing an Advanced Method
sections.objective: Resist the temptation to use the most impressive method available.

items.text: Start from the decision and the failure mode, not the technique.
Ask what a simpler baseline achieves first.
Estimate the cost: data, compute, monitoring, and maintenance.
Identify the assumption the method needs and test whether it holds.
Prefer the method whose failure mode you can detect in production.
Document the rejected methods and why they were rejected.
For five problems, propose an advanced method, a simple alternative, and the experiment that decides between them.
Reject one method on the grounds that its assumption fails in your data, and write the paragraph explaining it.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (11.10).** Every advanced method you adopt is justified against a simpler baseline and a detectable failure mode.

subBlocks.title: Project: `adv-ml-lab` — implement two, benchmark both, report honestly

elements.text: **Purpose.** Go deep on two advanced methods rather than skimming ten. Depth is what interviewers test, and depth is what makes a method usable.
**Choose two tracks** (one implementation-heavy, one analysis-heavy):

rows: deep ensembles, MC dropout, Laplace approximation, conformal wrapper
meta-learners, double ML, causal forest, uplift evaluation
global forecaster, deep probabilistic forecaster, survival model
contextual bandit, off-policy evaluation, recommender ranking
domain adaptation, importance weighting, OOD detection
Pareto frontier, constrained training, cost-aware inference

items.text: A from-scratch implementation of the core estimator or objective.
Validation against a reference implementation or a known ground truth (simulation).
A simple baseline that could plausibly be enough.
A controlled comparison: metric, cost, and failure mode.
Assumption checklist: what must hold for the method to be valid.
A short decision memo: adopt, reject, or adopt with conditions.
A benchmark harness that runs both studies reproducibly.
Results tables with intervals and compute cost.
A written analysis of one case where the advanced method did not beat the baseline.

elements.code:
adv-ml-lab/
├── conf/
│   ├── uncertainty.yaml
│   └── causality.yaml            # or whichever two tracks
├── src/adv_ml/
│   ├── uncertainty/{ensembles,mc_dropout,laplace,conformal}.py
│   ├── causality/{meta_learners,dml,uplift}.py
│   ├── sequences/{forecasters,survival}.py
│   ├── decisions/{bandits,ope,rankers}.py
│   ├── robustness/{shift,adaptation,ood}.py
│   ├── baselines.py
│   ├── evaluate.py
│   └── report.py
├── reports/
│   ├── study_a.md
│   ├── study_b.md
│   ├── assumptions.md
│   └── decisions.md
└── tests/

rows: Core estimator written from scratch, not only imported
Matches a reference or known truth within a stated tolerance
A simple alternative trained and reported
Every assumption listed with a test or a stated reason it cannot be tested
Training and inference cost reported for both approaches
At least one honest case where the advanced method did not win

items.text: Implement a third method in a different track and cross-compare.
Add a simulation study measuring estimator bias and coverage across 500 replications.
Deploy one method behind a small API with a latency budget.
Write the adoption memo as if to a sceptical engineering manager.

rows: Two methods implemented and validated, not skimmed
Baselines, intervals, seed variance, and assumption checks
At least one negative or mixed result reported plainly
Full regeneration from config and seeds

elements.text: Level 11 is complete when you can defend an advanced method's assumptions, cost, and failure modes against a simpler alternative — and admit when the simple one wins.

questions.question: What is the difference between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty?
How do deep ensembles estimate uncertainty, and what do they cost?
Why can a well-calibrated model still be badly wrong on OOD inputs?
When would you use conformal prediction instead of a Bayesian method?
How would you route low-confidence predictions to humans?
What is the fundamental problem of causal inference?
What is a confounder, and how do you adjust for one?
When is a T-learner inappropriate?
What are the assumptions of double machine learning?
How do you evaluate an uplift model without ground truth?
Why can a highly accurate model produce a badly biased effect estimate?
Why is random cross-validation invalid for time series?
What is MASE, and why use it over MAPE?
When would you use a global forecaster over per-series models?
What is a contextual bandit, and how does it differ from an A/B test?
What must you log to do off-policy evaluation?
Why is a two-stage recommender architecture common?
What is position bias, and how does it affect training data?
Name three types of distribution shift with an example each.
How does importance weighting correct for covariate shift, and what goes wrong?
Why do OOD detection benchmarks fail to transfer?
Which advanced method would you use for a decision with asymmetric costs?
When would you deliberately not use an advanced method?
How do you present a multi-objective trade-off to a product team?
Your causal estimate conflicts with an A/B test. What do you do?

items.text: I can separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty and choose a method accordingly.
I can fit and critique Gaussian process models.
I can forecast with correct temporal validation and calibrated intervals.
I can state an estimand, identification assumption, and estimator for a causal question.
I can design and evaluate a bandit or recommender system.
I can name and mitigate the distribution shift my system faces.
I can present a multi-objective frontier and defend an operating point.
I have implemented two advanced methods from scratch.
I have validated them against a reference or simulated truth.
I have compared each against a simple baseline with intervals.
I have reported one honest negative result.
I have written assumption and decision memos.
`adv-ml-lab` passes every acceptance target.
The assumptions document is specific and testable.
I can explain when I would reject my own chosen method.

elements.text: **Level 11 completion rule.** If you can implement an advanced method, state its assumptions, measure its cost, and admit when it loses, you are ready for Level 12.

levels.title: RESEARCH METHODS AND EXPERIMENTAL SCIENCE
levels.goal: Learn to produce knowledge, not just models: read papers critically, design experiments that can fail, reproduce results honestly, and write claims that your evidence actually supports.
levels.prerequisites: Levels 6 and 11. Evaluation discipline is the entry ticket; advanced methods give you something worth studying.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: Git, DVC, experiment tracking, LaTeX or Markdown, a reference manager, `pytest`, compute accounting
dashboard.main project: **`research-repro`** — reproduce a published result, ablate it, and write a 4-page report
dashboard.final outcome: Read, reproduce, critique, and communicate an ML result at the standard expected of an applied scientist.

sections.title: Thinking Like a Researcher
sections.objective: Replace "what technique can I use?" with "what claim am I testing?".

modules.title: From curiosity to a testable question

items.text: Observable phenomenon, hypothesised mechanism, and a falsifiable prediction.
The three question types: does it work, why does it work, and when does it fail.
Scoping a question to your compute and time budget.
The difference between a research question and a product question.
Writing the question before the experiment, in one sentence.

elements.latex:
\text{claim}:\ \theta \in \Theta_0\ \text{versus}\ \theta \in \Theta_1
\quad\text{with a pre-specified test and stopping rule}

items.text: Turn three vague curiosities into falsifiable hypotheses with a stated experiment.
Rewrite one hypothesis so that it could be disproved by a single run.
Recognising an important question versus an easy one.
The value of a negative result.
Incremental versus structural contributions.
Choosing problems where your constraints are an advantage.
Avoiding the "new dataset, same model" trap.
Read three abstracts and rank them by expected value of the result, with reasons.
Identify one question in your current work that nobody has answered well, and why.
Write the plan before running: hypothesis, metric, data, analysis, stopping rule.
Commit the plan to version control with a timestamp.
Distinguish confirmatory from exploratory analysis.
Report exploratory findings as exploratory.
The cost of skipping this: HARKing and unreportable results.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.1).** You can write a one-page experiment plan that someone else could execute and that could fail.

sections.title: Reading and Mapping Literature
sections.objective: Extract what a paper actually shows, efficiently.

items.text: **Pass 1 (5 min):** title, abstract, figures, conclusion — decide whether to continue.
**Pass 2 (30 min):** method, experiments, and the claims table; skip proofs.
**Pass 3 (2 h):** reproduce the argument line by line; question every assumption.
Extracting: claim, evidence, baseline, dataset, compute, and limitations.
Separating what was shown from what was implied.
Three-pass three papers and record the time each pass took and what you learned.
Write a 150-word summary of one paper's contribution and one thing it does not show.
Building a citation graph forwards and backwards.
Identifying the canonical baselines and the datasets in a subfield.
Finding the paper that everyone cites but nobody reproduces.
Tracking a subfield: venues, labs, and the few people who set the agenda.
Maintaining a paper log with structured notes.
Build a 20-paper map for one subfield with arrows for "improves on" and "evaluated on".
Identify three open problems from the map, each testable in a month.
Baseline fairness: were they tuned? at equal compute?
Statistical reporting: seeds, intervals, and number of runs.
Ablations: do they isolate the claimed cause?
Dataset leakage and benchmark contamination.
The gap between the abstract and the results table.
Red flags: single-seed gains, missing baselines, "we leave to future work" for the central question.
Find three specific weaknesses in a recent paper and state the experiment that would expose each.
Rewrite a paper's abstract so it matches its evidence exactly.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.2).** You can summarise, critique, and place a paper in its literature in under an hour.

sections.title: Reproducibility Science
sections.objective: Make your work, and other people's, actually reproducible.

items.text: Repeatability: same code, same data, same result.
Reproducibility: same method, independent implementation.
Replicability: same claim, new data.
Robustness: same conclusion across reasonable variations.
Which level your claim needs, and which you actually achieved.
Classify five published results by the level of evidence they actually provide.
State the level your own capstone achieves and what would raise it.
Code release with a working entry point and a small sample dataset.
Environment lockfiles and container images.
Data availability: licensing, access restrictions, and versioning.
Compute reporting: hardware, hours, and cost.
Model cards and datasheets.
Checklists: NeurIPS reproducibility checklist as a template for your own work.
Take an old project and produce a release that a stranger can run in under 15 minutes.
Write the compute-and-data section for your capstone before you finish it.
Reproducing from a paper: matching splits, preprocessing, and evaluation code.
Common gaps: undocumented preprocessing, undisclosed hyperparameters, different metric implementations.
When the gap is legitimate (missing compute) and when it is not (different test set).
Contacting authors with a precise, respectful discrepancy report.
Documenting what reproduced and what did not, with tolerances.

elements.latex:
\text{reproduction gap}=\left\lvert \text{reported metric}-\text{reproduced metric}\right\rvert
\quad\text{relative to the reported value}

items.text: Reproduce one small result and document every deviation from the paper.
Write a discrepancy report that a reader could verify in ten minutes.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.3).** You have reproduced one published result and documented the gaps precisely.

sections.title: Designing Experiments and Ablations
sections.objective: Build experiments that isolate causes and can produce a clean negative result.

items.text: One variable at a time, or a factorial design if interactions matter.
Matched compute, matched parameters, matched tuning effort.
Randomisation and blocking where applicable.
The confound that ruins most ML comparisons: unequal hyperparameter tuning.
Sanity checks and negative controls.

elements.latex:
\text{factorial design: } 2^k\ \text{runs for }k\text{ binary factors},\quad
\text{main effect}_A=\bar y_{A=1}-\bar y_{A=0}

items.text: Design a 2×2 factorial experiment for two design choices and analyse the main effects.
Identify the confound in a published comparison and propose the corrected design.
Ablate the claimed cause, not everything.
Report the ablation table with the main result, not in an appendix.
Variance across seeds is part of the result.
Ablation budgets: how many runs can you afford, and how do you spend them.
Control ablations: removing a component that should not matter.
Write an ablation plan for a model with four components, with a budget of 12 runs.
Show one control ablation that confirms your result is not an artefact.

modules.title: Multiple comparisons and researcher degrees of freedom

items.text: The garden of forking paths in ML: preprocessing, seeds, metrics, and stopping.
Correcting for multiple comparisons, or pre-registering a single primary metric.
Reporting all configurations you ran, not just the winner.
Exploratory versus confirmatory analysis, labelled explicitly.
Effect sizes, not just significance.
Simulate 40 configurations on pure noise and show the "best" improves over the baseline.
Present a results table that includes the failed configurations.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.4).** Your experiments isolate the cause you claim, and your tables show what did not work.

sections.title: Statistical Rigour in ML Research
sections.objective: Apply Phase 1's statistics to the specific pathologies of ML experiments.

items.text: Seed variance is often the largest term — measure it, do not assume it away.
Intervals for every headline metric; bootstrap across both seeds and examples.
Paired comparisons when runs share data or initialisation.
Correct for the number of comparisons in a sweep.
Report the number of runs, not just the mean.
Distinguish statistical from practical significance at the deployment decision.
Pre-specify the primary metric; treat the rest as secondary.
Beware of comparing against an untuned baseline — it is the most common inflation.
Re-analyse your Level 9 architecture comparison with paired tests and corrected comparisons.
Show a published-style "3% improvement" dissolving under seed variance.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.5).** Every claim you make is backed by an interval, a run count, and an appropriate test.

sections.title: Scientific Writing and Figures
sections.objective: Communicate so that the reader can verify your claims quickly.

items.text: Title, abstract, introduction, related work, method, experiments, limitations, conclusion.
The abstract as claim + evidence + implication, in 150 words.
The introduction's job: problem, gap, contribution, result.
Related work as positioning, not a list.
The limitations section as a mark of confidence, not weakness.
Write the abstract for your capstone before running the final experiments, then revise it to match the evidence.
Rewrite a weak related-work paragraph as positioning against two specific baselines.
One message per figure; the caption carries the claim.
Error bars and what they represent (std, std error, interval — say which).
Tables: the main result first, ablations second, honesty throughout.
Consistent colours, fonts, and units; readable at print size.
Plot choices: no 3D pies, no dual axes without warning, no truncated y-axes.
Every figure reproducible from a script.
Take one of your result tables and rebuild the figure so the claim is visible in five seconds.
Label every error bar in your capstone with its exact meaning.
The 3-minute, 10-minute, and 45-minute versions of the same work.
Anticipating the five questions every audience asks.
Handling "why not the simpler thing?" with evidence.
Defending limitations without undermining the contribution.
Writing a rebuttal: concede, clarify, or refute, with data.
Present your work at three lengths and record the 3-minute version.
Answer five hostile questions in writing, with numbers.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.6).** A reader can grasp your claim, verify it from your tables, and see its limits, in five minutes.

sections.title: Peer Review and Critique
sections.objective: Review others' work and your own with the same standard.

items.text: Review structure: summary, strengths, weaknesses, questions, recommendation.
Separating correctness issues from presentation issues.
Checking the core claim against the evidence table.
Asking for the experiment that would settle a disagreement.
Reviewing your own work before submission, as an adversary.
Response to review: which points to concede, which to contest with data.
The reviewer's obligation: be specific, be verifiable, be kind.
Write a full review of a recent paper in the standard format.
Swap a draft with a peer and review each other's capstone reports.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.7).** You can write a review that the authors could act on, and you can defend your own work against one.

sections.title: Benchmarks, Leaderboards and Contamination
sections.objective: Understand how benchmarks fail, and design evaluations that do not.

items.text: Benchmark saturation: when improvements are noise.
Contamination: test data in pretraining corpora, and how to test for it.
Leaderboard overfitting and the "test set in the wild" problem.
Benchmark design: coverage, difficulty stratification, and adversarial cases.
Private and rotating test sets; held-out evaluation services.
Goodhart's law in ML evaluation.
Building a domain benchmark that will not saturate in six months.
Test one model for contamination using a canary-string or memorisation probe.
Design a small domain benchmark with difficulty tiers and a contamination policy.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.8).** You can evaluate on public benchmarks without confusing leaderboard rank for capability.

sections.title: Research Engineering
sections.objective: Build the infrastructure that makes good science cheap.

items.text: A single config-driven entry point for every experiment.
A run registry: config, seed, commit, metrics, artefacts, compute.
Sweep orchestration with failure recovery and pruning.
Analysis scripts that read the registry and emit tables and figures.
Immutable evaluation sets with an access log.
Cost tracking per experiment and per project.
The habit: no result exists until it is in the registry and reproducible by a script.
Refactor one project into registry-driven experiments with generated tables.
Rebuild a past result from the registry alone, without touching a notebook.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.9).** Any number you can quote can be regenerated by running one script against the registry.

sections.title: Ethics, Safety and Societal Impact
sections.objective: Reason about consequences, not just metrics.

items.text: Dual use: the same model for detection and evasion.
Harm taxonomies: misclassification harm, allocation harm, representational harm.
Data provenance, consent, and licensing for research datasets.
Reproducibility as an ethical obligation when results inform policy.
Publication decisions: what not to release, and how to release it responsibly.
Differential privacy for released statistics.
Institutional review and human-subjects considerations.
Writing an impact statement that says something real.
Write an impact statement for your capstone that names two specific harms and one mitigation.
Assess whether a dataset you use could be used to harm the people in it.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.10).** Your work includes a specific, non-generic discussion of harms and mitigations.
**Purpose.** Produce the single strongest portfolio artefact for applied-science roles: evidence that you can read research, rebuild it, test its claims, and communicate the outcome honestly.

items.text: Code available, modest compute, one clear headline metric.
Ideally a paper whose claim you find slightly suspicious.
Rebuild the evaluation protocol exactly: splits, preprocessing, metric implementation.
Match the reported headline number within a stated tolerance, or document precisely why not.
Record every deviation in a deviations table.
Report compute used, hardware, and wall-clock time.
Identify the paper's central claim and design the ablation that tests it.
At least three ablations, each varying one component, across at least two seeds.
Include one control ablation that should show no effect.
Report mean and spread, not single runs.
Evidence table: claim, evidence in the paper, evidence in your reproduction, verdict.
Threats to validity: baseline tuning, contamination, seed variance, dataset limits.
One proposed experiment that would settle the biggest open question.
Abstract with claim, method, result, and limitation.
Method summary and deviations.
Results table beside the paper's numbers.
Ablation table with spread.
Limitations and impact statement.
Reproduction instructions sufficient for a stranger.
Repository with one-command reproduction, pinned environment, and sample data.
The report rendered as a shareable PDF or Markdown.

items.text: Contact the authors with a precise discrepancy report and record the response.
Extend the method to a second dataset and see whether the claim holds.
Propose and run the experiment the paper left to future work.
Submit the report to a workshop or a public writeup for real feedback.

elements.text: **Level 12 completion rule.** If someone else can verify your claim from your artefact, and your critique survives their disagreement, you are ready for Phase 5.

levels.title: NLP, COMPUTER VISION, AND FOUNDATION MODELS
levels.goal: Build real systems on top of foundation models: fine-tune for a domain, retrieve, ground, serve within a latency and cost budget, and evaluate against a domain eval set you built yourself.
levels.prerequisites: Levels 7–12. Especially: transformer implementation (9.4), fine-tuning mechanics (L8), evaluation protocol (L6, L12), and research honesty (L12).

dashboard.level: 13 — NLP, Computer Vision, and Foundation Models
dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: `transformers`, `peft`, `trl`, `datasets`, `vLLM`, `timm`, `ultralytics`, `diffusers`, `faiss`, `lm-evaluation-harness`
dashboard.main project: **`foundation-suite`** — an applied NLP assistant and an applied vision/VLM pipeline, both with eval suites and cost models
dashboard.final outcome: Build, evaluate, and serve foundation-model systems with measured quality, latency, and cost — and know when not to use a foundation model.

sections.title: The Applied NLP Landscape
sections.objective: Match the task to the cheapest approach that works, before reaching for a large model.

items.text: Classification, tagging, extraction, retrieval, ranking, summarisation, generation, and dialogue.
The baseline ladder: rules → TF-IDF + linear → fine-tuned encoder → prompted LLM → fine-tuned LLM.
Cost per 1,000 requests at each rung, and quality at each rung.
When a 10-minute baseline is the correct engineering decision.
Why most "LLM use cases" are actually classification or extraction.
Take three proposed "LLM features" and re-express them as classification or extraction tasks.
Build the full baseline ladder for one task and report quality and cost per rung.
Unicode normalisation, whitespace, casing, and language identification.
Handling code, numbers, identifiers, and mixed scripts (relevant for Indic languages).
Deduplication and near-duplicate detection at corpus level.
PII detection and redaction before sending text to any API.
Chunking for retrieval versus truncation for classification.
Build a preprocessing pipeline that handles English, Hindi, and code in the same corpus.
Show a case where aggressive preprocessing destroys signal.
Labelling protocols and inter-annotator agreement.

sections.title: Context, Memory and Agents
sections.objective: Build systems that hold state and use tools without becoming unpredictable.

modules.title: Workflows versus agents and stateful control graphs

items.text: Single LLM call vs deterministic workflow/DAG vs autonomous agent loop: deciding based on path predictability, latency, and cost.
The ReAct loop ($\text{thought} \rightarrow \text{action} \rightarrow \text{observation}$) versus plan-and-execute architectures; implementing the loop in raw Python before using any framework.
Stateful graph orchestration (`LangGraph` / explicit state machines): typed state schemas, conditional edges, bounded retry loops, and checkpoint persistence to resume interrupted runs.
Multi-agent decomposition (orchestrator–worker, sequential handoffs, parallel specialists) and when a single agent with well-designed tools is faster, cheaper, and more reliable.
Human-in-the-loop interrupts and approval gates before executing consequential or irreversible actions.

elements.latex: P(\text{success over } k \text{ autonomous steps}) = p^k \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{per-step reliability compounds exponentially}

items.text: Implement the same 3-step research-and-extraction task both as a fixed DAG workflow and as an autonomous ReAct agent; compare task accuracy, p95 latency, and token cost across 30 runs.
Build a checkpointed state-machine graph that pauses for human approval before a write action and resumes cleanly from saved state after interruption.

modules.title: Tool protocols (MCP), untrusted arguments, and sandboxed execution

items.text: Designing high-signal tool interfaces: unambiguous names, minimal typed parameters (`Pydantic` / JSON Schema), bounded return payloads, and actionable error messages for self-correction.

Model Context Protocol (`MCP`): host $\rightarrow$ client $\rightarrow$ server architecture, exposing external databases/APIs as standardized tools and resources, local (`stdio`) vs remote (`SSE`/HTTP) transports, and trust boundaries.

Treating all model-generated tool arguments as untrusted input: schema validation, permission scoping, read-only vs mutating tool separation, and idempotency keys so retries never duplicate side effects.

Sandboxed code and command execution: running model-generated Python/Bash inside isolated containers or microVMs (`Docker`, `Modal`, `E2B`) with strict CPU, memory, timeout, filesystem, and network restrictions.
Build an `MCP` server exposing a read-only query tool and a mutating action tool with strict schema validation and idempotency protection.
Execute model-generated Python data-analysis snippets inside an isolated container sandbox with a 5-second timeout and no outbound network access, returning captured `stdout`/`stderr` to the loop.

modules.title: Context compaction, memory systems, and trajectory evaluation

items.text: Context budget accounting across turns: system instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool schemas, tool outputs, and generation headroom.
Managing context growth over long runs: sliding windows, rolling summarisation, and offloading large tool outputs out of the active prompt.
Memory architectures: short-term working state (scratchpad) versus long-term persistent memory (episodic past runs, semantic user/domain facts) and the `write → retrieve → update → forget` lifecycle.
End-to-end trajectory observability: tracing every model call, tool invocation, token count, latency, and retry in a single execution trace.

Evaluating agents rigorously: end-to-end task success rate, $\text{pass}@k$ vs $\text{pass}\text{\textasciicircum}k$ consistency across repeated trials, tool-selection accuracy, step efficiency, and cost per solved task.
Build a tool-using agent with rolling context compaction, a hard step/cost ceiling, and full trace logging; diagnose three distinct failure modes from traces alone.
Evaluate your agent on a 30-task benchmark reporting $\text{pass}@1$, $\text{pass}\text{\textasciicircum}3$ reliability, average steps, and USD cost per completed task.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (13.6).** Your agent uses validated/sandboxed tools, has bounded context and cost, persists state across interrupts, and is evaluated on multi-trial task success ($\text{pass}\text{\textasciicircum}k$).

elements.text: **Level 13 completion rule.** If you can build, evaluate, afford, secure, and operate foundation-model systems, you are ready to specialise in Level 14.

levels.title: APPLIED ML RESEARCH SPECIALIZATION
levels.goal: Choose a specialisation, build command of its literature, produce one real contribution, and publish it in a form that survives review. This level is about becoming known for something specific.
levels.prerequisites: Levels 10–13. You need research method (L12), advanced methods (L11), and applied command of the frontier (L13).

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: Git, DVC, experiment registry, LaTeX/Markdown, arXiv, OpenReview, Hugging Face Hub
dashboard.main project: **`specialist-thesis`** — a focused contribution with a public write-up, code, and eval suite
dashboard.final outcome: Own a specialisation: know its literature, produce a defensible result, and release it so others can build on it.

sections.title: Choosing and Defining a Specialisation
sections.objective: Pick a lane you can defend for years, not a topic you can finish in a week.

items.text: Axis 1 — modality: language, vision, audio, tabular, multimodal.
Axis 2 — problem: representation, generation, retrieval, decision, evaluation.
Axis 3 — constraint: low resource, low latency, privacy, multilingual, scientific.
Axis 4 — role: systems builder, method developer, evaluation scientist, domain translator.
Choosing two axes and going deep is better than touching five.
Examples of coherent specialisations: low-resource Indic NLP, medical imaging under shift, evaluation of agentic systems, embedded vision, tabular causal ML.
Draw your own axes and place five candidate specialisations on them.
Eliminate three options with a stated reason each (data access, competition, interest).
Data access: what you can legally and practically obtain.
Compute budget: what you can run in a week without a cluster.
Domain access: can you talk to practitioners who have the problem?
Competition: is this crowded with well-funded labs?
Career fit: does this specialisation exist as a role where you want to work?
Time to signal: how long before you have something showable?
Write a one-page constraint sheet: data, compute, time, access, and career target.
Reject one specialisation on constraint grounds and document why.
Level 1: reproduce an existing result in a new domain.
Level 2: a careful evaluation showing a claim does not hold.
Level 3: a small methodological improvement with ablations.
Level 4: a new dataset, benchmark, or evaluation protocol.
Level 5: a structural insight that changes how others work.
Most valuable first contributions are Level 1–2; they are also the most credible.
Choose the contribution level you can realistically reach in eight weeks.
Explain why a Level 2 evaluation contribution is publishable when done well.

sections.title: Writing the Thesis Paper
sections.objective: Produce a workshop-quality paper that a reviewer can verify.

items.text: Title that states the claim, not the technique.
Abstract: context, gap, method, result with a number, implication.
Introduction: the problem matters, the gap is real, the contribution is specific.
Related work as positioning against three named baselines.
Method described so it can be reimplemented.
Results: main table, ablations, and negative controls.
Limitations and threats to validity, written honestly.
Impact statement and safety considerations.
Appendix: full hyperparameters, compute, and data details.
Write the paper in this order: figures → results → method → introduction → abstract.
Have a peer mark every sentence that is not supported by a number or a citation.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (14.7).** A peer can state your claim after reading only your abstract and first figure.

sections.title: Releasing Artefacts
sections.objective: Make your work usable, which is what makes it matter.

items.text: Repository: README with install, reproduce, and citation.
Pinned environment and a one-command reproduction of the main table.
Model or dataset card with intended use and limits.

Public demo with a hard cost ceiling.
Versioning and a changelog; a plan for issues.
Licence compatible with your dependencies and data.
Citation block and a permanence plan (DOI via Zenodo or similar).
Publish a repository that reproduces your main table in under 30 minutes on a rented GPU.
Add a demo with a five-dollar-per-day hard cap and measure the cost per session.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (14.8).** A stranger can reproduce your headline result from your release without contacting you.

sections.title: Applied Research Inside a Company
sections.objective: Do rigorous work under real constraints.

items.text: Aligning a research question with a business decision.
The 20% exploration budget and how to protect it.
IP, publication approval, and disclosure risk.
Working with product teams: timelines, expectations, and scope creep.
Turning a research result into a product decision (reuse L6.10).
Internal write-ups as first-class artefacts, even when nothing publishes.
Measuring success by the decisions your work changed, not by papers.
Write an internal research proposal with a business decision attached to each experiment.
Draft a disclosure review note for a result you want to publish.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (14.9).** Your research plan names the decision each experiment informs.

sections.title: Building Reputation Without Self-Promotion
sections.objective: Become findable by doing visible work.

items.text: Open-source contributions that solve other people's problems.
Writing that explains, not announces: technical posts with numbers.
Talks and meetups; the 10-minute version of your work.
Reproducibility challenges and public benchmarking.
Answering questions in communities where your users are.
A personal index page: projects, papers, demos, and contact.
Consistency over intensity: one artefact per month beats one burst per year.
Write one technical post that explains a negative result you got.
Make one open-source contribution to a library you use in your thesis.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (14.10).** You have a public artefact trail a hiring manager can follow.

sections.title: Staying Current Without Drowning
sections.objective: Maintain command of a moving field sustainably.

items.text: A reading cadence: 3 papers a week, one deep read.
Curated sources over feeds: venue proceedings, a handful of labs, two newsletters.
Quarterly re-assessment of your gap analysis.
A 15-minute rule for testing a new claim: find the baseline and the seeds.
Deliberately ignoring popular topics that do not affect your specialisation.
Re-evaluating your specialisation annually against the job market.
Build your weekly reading system and run it for the duration of this level.
Test three new claims with the 15-minute rule and record verdicts.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (14.11).** You have a sustainable system and evidence you are using it.
**Purpose.** Produce the artefact that lets you say "I work on X" and be believed: a focused, reproducible contribution in a specialisation you have chosen deliberately.

items.text: A reproduction plus extension in a new domain.

A small methodological improvement with ablations and a control.
A new dataset, benchmark, or evaluation protocol with a datasheet.

Dataset or model card, if applicable.
Eval harness released alongside results.
4–8 page workshop-style paper with figures, ablations, limitations, and impact statement.
A 10-minute talk with slides, recorded.
Published to arXiv, a workshop, a blog with code, or an open review venue.
A short thread or post explaining the result to practitioners.

levels.title: END-TO-END ML ENGINEERING AND MLOPS
levels.goal: Take a model you built and make it a service you can operate: reproducible training, versioned artefacts, safe deployment, real monitoring, automated retraining, and runbooks that work at 2 a.m.

sections.title: Requirements and Design Before Code
sections.objective: Decide what "working" means before choosing tools.

items.text: Latency: p50, p95, p99 budgets, and which one the product cares about.
Throughput: requests per second at peak, and burstiness.
Freshness: how stale a prediction may be.
Availability target and the cost of downtime in currency.
Cost per 1,000 predictions, and the unit economics of the product.
Data residency, retention, and audit requirements.
Write NFRs for a fraud-scoring service with numbers, and state the cost of missing each.

Problem, users, and the decision the model changes.
Data sources, freshness, and ownership.
Training and serving architecture, with a diagram.

Failure modes and the fallback for each.
Rollout plan, monitoring plan, and rollback plan.
Alternatives considered and rejected, with reasons.
Write a two-page design doc for a model service and have a peer attack every box.
List ten failure modes and the specific detection for each.
Batch scoring: cheapest, highest latency tolerance.
Real-time request/response: the default for interactive products.
Streaming: events and continuous scoring.
Edge/on-device: privacy and latency, at the cost of updates.
Hybrid: precompute candidates, rank in real time.
Matching the pattern to the freshness and latency requirement.

sections.title: Reproducible Training Pipelines
sections.objective: Make training a repeatable job, not a person.

items.text: Stages: ingest → validate → transform → train → evaluate → register → deploy.
Idempotency: re-running a stage must not duplicate or corrupt.
Caching and partial reruns.
Artefacts between stages: data snapshots, feature sets, models, metrics.
Orchestrators: Airflow, Dagster, Prefect, Kubeflow, or plain cron with discipline.
Parameterisation and environment separation.

Point-in-time correctness enforced in the pipeline, not by convention.

Determinism trade-offs on GPU.

Reproducing a production model from its registry entry alone.

Record everything that made the run different the second time.

Naming and grouping runs so humans can find them.

Retention and cost of tracking servers.

Stages or aliases: staging, shadow, canary, production, archived.
Promotion criteria: metric thresholds, slice checks, data checks, security review.

Rollback as a pointer change, not a rebuild.

Roll back to the previous version and prove predictions are identical.
Container images as the unit of deployment.
Base-image pinning and reproducible builds.
Model artefacts versus image-embedded models: trade-offs.

sections.title: Serving and Inference Engineering
sections.objective: Serve predictions with predictable latency and cost.

items.text: API contract: request/response schema, validation, error codes.
Batching: static versus dynamic and the latency/throughput trade-off.
Concurrency model: sync workers, async, and worker pools.
Warm-up, model loading, and cold-start behaviour.
Timeouts, retries, and idempotency keys.
Graceful degradation: cheap model, cached answer, or rule-based fallback.
Load test a service at 1×, 5×, and 10× expected traffic and record p50/p95/p99.
Add dynamic batching for a GPU service and report the throughput gain and latency cost.
Own servers, managed endpoints, serverless, and batch transforms.
GPU utilisation and the cost of idle capacity.
Quantisation and distillation for serving (reuse 9.8).

Multi-model serving and per-tenant isolation.
Choosing the cheapest option that meets the latency SLO.

Prediction caching and cache-key design (including feature freshness).

Batch offline work to spot instances.

Measuring cost per successful prediction after retries.

sections.title: Deployment Strategies
sections.objective: Change production without breaking it.

items.text: Shadow deployment: run the new model on live traffic without acting on it.
Canary: route a small percentage, compare guardrails, then widen.
Blue/green: instant switch and instant rollback.
Feature flags for model selection, including per-segment rollout.
Rollback triggers: error rate, latency, and guardrail metrics.
Model and feature compatibility during rollout — the subtle failure.
Database and schema migrations that cannot break the previous version.
A tested rollback: a rollback you have not run is a wish.
Ship a model change as a canary with automatic rollback on a guardrail breach.
Break backwards compatibility deliberately and prove the rollback still works.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (15.5).** You have executed a canary rollout and a rollback, and can state the metric that triggered it.

sections.title: Monitoring and Observability
sections.objective: Find out about problems before users do.

items.text: **System:** latency percentiles, error rates, saturation, queue depth.

Thresholds, windows, and burn-rate alerts for SLOs.
Alert fatigue and how to fix it (deletion is a feature).
Runbooks: symptom, diagnosis steps, mitigation, escalation.

sections.objective: Keep the model good after launch.

levels.title: ML SYSTEMS AND SCALABILITY
levels.goal: Design ML systems that survive scale, failure, and change — and defend those designs under interview conditions. This is the level that decides senior-versus-junior in system design rounds.
levels.prerequisites: Level 15. You cannot design a system you have never operated; every design claim in this level should be traceable to something you built.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: Whiteboard, back-of-envelope maths, queueing intuition, your L15 build as evidence
dashboard.main project: **`system-design-vault`** — three full designs plus one load-tested implementation
dashboard.final outcome: Produce a complete, defensible ML system design in 45 minutes, with numbers for scale, latency, cost, and failure.

sections.title: The Design Framework
sections.objective: Have a repeatable structure so you never ramble in a design interview.

items.text: **Clarify** — users, decisions, scale, latency, freshness, cost, constraints.
**Frame** — prediction target, label source, feedback loop, offline versus online.
**Data** — sources, volume, quality, labelling plan, point-in-time needs.
**Model** — baseline, candidate approaches, evaluation, why this one.
**Serve** — architecture, stages, caching, degradation, latency budget.
**Operate** — monitoring, retraining, drift, on-call, rollback.
**Trade-offs** — what you gave up, what breaks at 10×/100×, and what you would do first.
Write the seven headings on a card and rehearse using them against three prompts.
Time-box each step for a 45-minute interview (5/5/10/10/8/4/3 minutes).
User scale and requests per second — the first question that matters.
Latency tolerance: 20 ms, 200 ms, and 2 s lead to different architectures.
Freshness: seconds versus hours changes feature and serving design.
Cost ceiling per prediction and per month.
Data availability: do labels exist, and how late do they arrive?
Regulatory and privacy constraints that forbid an option entirely.

rows: precomputed features, no cross-encoder, small model
no PII may leave the region

items.text: For one product, write three requirement sets that would produce three different designs.
Identify the requirement that eliminates the most expensive option, and say so out loud.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.1).** You can run the seven steps in 45 minutes, in order, without skipping requirements.

sections.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
sections.objective: Put numbers on a whiteboard before drawing boxes.

items.text: QPS from daily active users and actions per session.
Peak factor: typically 2–5× average, and what drives the peak.
Storage: rows × bytes × replication × retention.
Model size and memory: parameters × bytes per parameter.
Compute: FLOPs per inference and the hardware's effective throughput.
Network: payload size × QPS.
Cost: instance-hour rate × count, plus storage and egress.
Estimate QPS, storage, and GPU count for a feed-ranking system at 10M DAU.
Show the arithmetic for a model that must fit in 16 GB of VRAM, including KV cache.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.2).** You can produce credible QPS, storage, memory, and cost numbers in under five minutes, out loud.

sections.title: Training Systems at Scale
sections.objective: Design the pipeline that produces models, not just the one that serves them.

items.text: Data ingestion volume and throughput requirements.
Distributed training strategy: data, tensor, pipeline, and sharding.
Checkpointing strategy and cost of the checkpoint interval.
Experiment throughput: how many runs per week can the system support?
Feature computation at scale: offline batch versus streaming.
Label pipelines and their latency.
Cost model for training: GPU-hours per model version.
Reproducibility across a fleet of heterogeneous workers.

elements.latex:
\text{train cost}=\text{GPU-hours}\times\text{hourly rate},\qquad
\text{GPU-hours}=\frac{\text{total tokens}\times\text{FLOPs per token}}{\text{hardware throughput}\times\text{utilisation}}

items.text: Estimate the GPU-hours to retrain a model weekly for a year, and the annual cost.
Design a training pipeline that supports 50 experiment runs per week without queueing chaos.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.3).** You can state the training cost of a model version and justify the retraining cadence.

sections.title: Serving and Inference at Scale
sections.objective: Scale the request path without breaking latency.

items.text: Break the budget per stage: gateway, auth, feature fetch, model, post-process, serialisation.
Fan-out cost: five downstream calls at p99 each combine badly.
Tail at scale: one slow shard determines the request's p99.
Hedged requests and their cost.
Caching layers and where they sit.

elements.latex:
\text{combined }p99\approx\max_i p99_i\ \text{for serial stages};\qquad
\text{fan-out of }k\text{ calls worsens the tail with }k

items.text: Build a latency budget table for a request with six stages and a 200 ms p95 SLO.
Compute how a 5 ms p99 feature call becomes a 40 ms problem under fan-out of 20.
Two-stage architecture: retrieve cheaply, rank expensively.
Candidate sources: popularity, collaborative, embedding ANN, rules.
Recall ceiling: the ranking stage cannot fix what retrieval missed.
ANN index trade-offs: recall versus latency versus memory.
Multi-stage ranking and the marginal value of each stage.
Specify a retrieval plan for 100M items with a 10 ms budget per query.
Compute how much of the recall ceiling the ranker can actually recover.
Horizontal scaling, sharding, and partitioning by entity.
Hot keys and celebrity problems; mitigation by replication and caching.
Queueing: async inference and the user-experience cost of waiting.
Autoscaling lag and pre-warming during a traffic spike.
GPU pooling, multi-model serving, and isolation between tenants.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.4).** You can defend a serving design under "what breaks at 100×?" without hand-waving.

sections.title: Data Systems for ML
sections.objective: Design storage and pipelines that feed training and serving correctly.

items.text: Lake, warehouse, and lakehouse choices and their consequences.
Batch versus streaming pipelines, and their latency/cost curves.
Feature store concepts: offline/online parity, point-in-time joins, TTL.
Event schema design and evolution.
Data quality gates and quarantine paths.
Retention, archival, and the cost of keeping everything.
Backfill strategy and its interaction with model versioning.
Design the data flow for features that must be identical in training and serving.
Plan a backfill that does not corrupt online state.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.5).** You can explain how a feature reaches both training and serving identically, with a diagram.

sections.title: Reliability Engineering for ML
sections.objective: Design for failure you have not personally seen.

items.text: Failure taxonomy: dependency, capacity, data, model, and human error.
Graceful degradation ladder: full model → smaller model → cached → heuristic → refuse.
Timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers, and bulkheads.
Idempotency for writes and scoring requests.
Blast radius reduction: per-tenant quotas and feature flags.
Failover between regions and providers.
Chaos experiments you can actually run.

rows: reduce batch, restart, route to replica

items.text: Design a degradation ladder for a fraud system and state the precision cost of each rung.
Run a failure-injection test and measure whether degradation or outage occurred.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.6).** Every dependency in your design has a failure mode, a detection, and a defined degraded behaviour.

sections.title: Cost and Capacity Modelling
sections.objective: Know what the system costs before it exists.

items.text: Unit economics: cost per prediction, per user, per 1,000 requests.
Cost drivers ranked, with the largest one addressed first.
Fixed versus variable cost, and how the mix changes with scale.
Break-even analysis for a new model or feature.
Reserved versus on-demand versus spot capacity.
The hidden costs: monitoring, storage growth, egress, and on-call time.
Build a cost model spreadsheet for a system at 1M, 10M, and 100M requests per month.
Find the request volume at which a cheaper model with more infrastructure becomes optimal.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.7).** You can produce a credible monthly cost model with a sensitivity analysis on the top driver.

sections.title: The Worked Designs
sections.objective: Practise the prompts that actually appear in interviews.

items.text: Candidate generation, ranking, re-ranking, and diversity constraints.
Cold start for users and items.
Feedback loops and position bias.
Evaluation: offline nDCG, online engagement, and long-term value.
Scale: 100M items, 10M users, p99 under 150 ms.
Deliver a full design in 45 minutes with QPS, storage, latency budget, and failure modes.
Prepare the "what breaks at 100×" answer in three sentences.
Extreme imbalance, adversarial drift, and label delay.
Rules plus model, and how they compose.
Real-time features with velocity windows.
Precision at a fixed alert budget and human review capacity.
Explainability requirements for adverse actions and appeals.
Design a fraud system where a false positive blocks a legitimate customer, and state the policy.
Quantify the cost of both error types and derive the threshold.
Retrieval architecture, ranking, and query understanding.
Permissions-aware retrieval and document isolation.
Index freshness and incremental updates.
Extraction pipelines with human review.
Latency budget for retrieval plus generation.
Design enterprise search across 50M documents with access control and a 300 ms budget.
Design an invoice pipeline at 5M documents per month with cost per document.
Serving stacks, continuous batching, and KV-cache economics.
Routing between models by task difficulty.
Prompt and response caching with correctness caveats.
Safety filtering in the request path and its latency cost.
Cost per task and the economics of the free tier.
Design a customer-support assistant serving 2M conversations per month with a cost ceiling.
Compute the KV-cache memory at 32k context and the maximum concurrent sessions.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.8).** You have delivered at least three of these designs aloud, with numbers, under a timer.

sections.title: Communicating Design
sections.objective: Make the drawing do the explaining.

items.text: Diagram conventions: data flow, training path, serving path, control plane, and observability.
Labelling with numbers, not adjectives.
Presenting trade-offs as tables, not prose.
Saying "I would measure X before choosing" instead of guessing.
Admitting unknowns without losing the thread.
Handling interruptions and returning to the structure.
Draw the same system twice: once for an engineer, once for a product stakeholder.
Present a design in ten minutes and count the questions you could not answer.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.9).** A reviewer can redraw your system from your explanation.

sections.title: Judgement Under Interview Conditions
sections.objective: Be assessed well, not just be right.

items.text: Clarify before designing; two minutes saves ten.
State assumptions explicitly and invite correction.
Choose a baseline architecture, then improve it out loud.
Prioritise: say what you would do first with limited time.
Answer the asked question, then add one valuable insight.
Stay honest: "I have not operated that at this scale; here is how I would reason about it."
Close with risks and next steps.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (16.10).** You can hold the seven-step frame under interruption without losing structure.

subBlocks.title: Project: `system-design-vault` — three designs and one build

elements.label: Purpose
elements.value: Produce a reusable, defensible design portfolio and back one design with a working, load-tested implementation.

elements.text: Choose three prompts from 16.8 (at least one from recommender/search, one from risk or document intelligence, one LLM system). Each design must include:

items.text: Requirements with numbers (QPS, latency, freshness, cost ceiling).
Back-of-envelope estimates for storage, compute, and memory.
Data and labelling plan, including delay.
Model approach with rejected alternatives.
Serving architecture diagram with per-stage latency budgets.
Monitoring and retraining plan.
Failure-mode table with detection and degradation.
Cost model at 1×, 10×, 100× scale.
Three questions you would be asked, with answers.
Implement a simplified but real version of one design.

Load test at 1×, 5×, and 10× expected traffic.
