elements.text: **Level 16 completion rule.** If you can design, quantify, defend, and degrade a system you have never built, you are ready for the final phase.

levels.title: PORTFOLIO AND RESEARCH CAPSTONE
levels.goal: Build a portfolio that survives the ten-minute hiring-manager scan: three projects that are each finished, measured, reproducible, and explained — plus one flagship that combines research rigour with production engineering.
levels.prerequisites: Levels 1–16. You need finished work; this level is about selection, packaging, and narrative, not new modelling.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: GitHub, Hugging Face Hub, a static site, Loom/OBS, `pandoc`/Markdown, LinkedIn, a resume builder
dashboard.main project: **`portfolio-pack`** — three curated projects, three case studies, one flagship capstone, one site, one video
dashboard.final outcome: A portfolio a stranger can evaluate in ten minutes and a hiring manager can champion in a review meeting.

sections.title: Portfolio Strategy
sections.objective: Decide what to show before you polish anything.

modules.title: What a hiring manager actually does

items.text: Opens your GitHub, reads one README, looks at commit history, closes the tab: that is the entire first pass.
Looks for: a real problem, a baseline, a measured result, a reproducible run, and a limitation stated honestly.
Discounts: tutorial clones, notebook dumps, leaderboard screenshots with no protocol, projects with no README.
Asks three questions: *can this person build, can this person measure, and can this person explain?*
Portfolio review is a filtering exercise, not a reading exercise.
Time yourself scanning three other people's portfolios and write down what you concluded in 60 seconds each.
Rewrite one of your own READMEs so the first screen answers "what, result, how to run".

elements.text: Choose three projects that collectively prove:

items.text: **You can build a system** — pipeline, service, deployment, monitoring.
**You can measure and model** — baselines, validation, calibration, error analysis.
**You can go deep** — research-grade rigour, or a foundation-model system with cost and safety.
One project should be in the domain you are targeting for work.
At most one should be a "clean classic" (churn, MNIST-adjacent) — and only if it is exceptionally well executed.
Depth beats breadth: three finished beats nine abandoned.
A fourth "flagship" project is allowed, but only after the three are done.
Inventory every project you have and score each on: finished, measured, reproducible, explained, relevant.
Select three and write one sentence on what each proves about you.
A one-line positioning statement: role + domain + evidence.
The order in which you present projects and why.
The through-line: what you keep choosing to work on.
What you deliberately exclude, and the story you tell if asked.
Consistency across resume, site, GitHub, and LinkedIn.

elements.latex: \text{positioning}=\text{role}+\text{domain}+\text{proof}\quad\text{e.g. "applied scientist, document intelligence, shipped a measured extraction system at USD 0.004 per doc"}

items.text: Write three versions of your positioning statement and test them on a peer.
Make your resume headline, site subtitle, and GitHub bio say the same thing.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.1).** You have three selected projects and a one-sentence positioning that a stranger repeats back correctly.

sections.title: Auditing and Curating Existing Work
sections.objective: Decide what to fix, what to hide, and what to retire.

items.text: Audit each repository against the portfolio rubric (17.11).
Identify the single biggest gap per project: measurement, reproducibility, or explanation.
Delete or archive projects that weaken the narrative.
Fix the top project first; a strong one outranks four mediocre ones.
Remove secrets, PII, and leaked data from every repository (an old `config.py` with an API key is a real risk).
Check licences on datasets and pretrained models before showcasing.
Verify every claim in every README against a number you can reproduce today.
Run a secrets scan across all repositories and fix every hit.
Pick one old project, spend a day making it reproducible, and measure the improvement in how it reads.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.2).** Every repository you keep passes a secret scan and a five-minute reproduction check.

sections.title: Packaging a Project Properly
sections.objective: Make each project cheap to evaluate and cheap to trust.

modules.title: The README as a product page

items.text: **First screen:** what it is, the result with a number and an interval, and the one command to reproduce.
A figure that shows the result, not the architecture.
"Why this matters" in two sentences.
Quickstart that genuinely works from a clean clone.
Results table with baselines and intervals.
Limitations and failure modes, stated plainly.
Links: demo, video, case study, paper.

elements.code:
# Project name — one line on what it does
**Result:** 0.87 macro-F1 (95% CI 0.84–0.90), vs 0.71 baseline. Cost: USD 0.004 per document.
![results](figures/results.png)
## Quickstart
    make setup && make reproduce
## What it does / Why / How it works / Results / Limitations

items.text: Rewrite one README so a peer can state your result after ten seconds.
Get a stranger to run your quickstart and record where they got stuck.
Pinned environment, lockfile, and documented hardware.
Sample data included so the pipeline runs without private access.
One command for the headline result; a second for the full study.
Deterministic seeds and a tolerance for expected variation.
A CI badge that is actually green.
Rebuild your flagship on a fresh machine or a rented GPU using only the README.
Time the reproduction and put that number in the README.
A licence that matches your dependencies and data.
A citation block; a DOI via Zenodo if you want permanence.
Clean commit history that shows incremental work.
No large binaries in Git; use releases or object storage.
Issue templates and a contribution note if you want collaborators.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.3).** A stranger reproduces your headline result in under 30 minutes from the README alone.

sections.title: Case Studies
sections.objective: Write the six-part story that makes a project reviewable in three minutes.

items.text: **Problem and user** — who has this problem, and what decision changes?
**Constraint** — data, latency, cost, or privacy limit that shaped the design.
**Approach** — the baseline, the model, and the one non-obvious decision.
**Evidence** — the headline number with an interval, against a stated baseline.
**Failure** — the worst slice, the honest limitation, and what you would do next.
**Impact** — what it would change in production, in the user's units.
Write case studies for two projects at 600 words each.
Have a peer mark any sentence that is not backed by a number or a decision.
Choose a failure that is informative, not one that makes the project look broken.
Quantify it: which slice, how much worse, and at what cost.
Distinguish "I know why and it is fixable" from "I know why and it is inherent".
Show the diagnostic that found it.
Propose the next experiment.
Rewrite a failure section three times: too defensive, too self-critical, and calibrated.
Ask a peer which version they would trust in a hiring decision.
One page is a summary; three pages is a case study; the repository is the appendix.
Scannable headings; numbers in bold; no wall of prose.
One diagram, maximum, and it should be the system or the result.
Every case study ends with a link to the artefact.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.4).** A reviewer can explain your project's result and its main limitation after reading one page.

sections.title: Demos, Videos and Live Links
sections.objective: Let people experience the work without installing anything.

items.text: A 2–3 minute video: problem, demo, result, limitation. Script it, do not improvise.
Screen recording with captions; no background music; readable text at 720p.
A live demo with rate limits, a cost cap, and a clear "this is a demo" banner.
A deterministic demo mode with cached outputs, so a demo never fails during a review.
Accessibility: contrast, font size, and alt text.
A one-click path from README to video to demo.
Record three takes of a 2-minute demo and pick the one where the value is clear by 0:20.
Run the demo from a cold start and time how long it takes to show a result.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.6).** Someone can understand your project's value from a 2-minute video without reading anything else.

sections.title: Profile, Resume and Screening Surface
sections.objective: Make the first ten seconds work.

items.text: One page for under ten years of experience; two at most.
Header: name, role, location, links (GitHub, site, LinkedIn).
Summary line that matches your positioning statement.
Experience: action, method, metric, scale — every bullet has a number.
Projects: only the three, each one line plus links.
Skills: honest, grouped, and consistent with what you can be interviewed on.
Education and publications last, unless research is your differentiator.

elements.latex:
\text{bullet}=\text{verb}+\text{what}+\text{method}+\text{metric}+\text{scale}
\quad\text{e.g. "Cut inference cost 62\% by distilling a 7B model to 1.3B at equal F1"}

items.text: Rewrite five bullets so each contains a number and a mechanism.
Remove every technology you would not want to be interviewed on.
Pinned repositories: exactly the three, in narrative order.
Profile README with the positioning line and links.
A simple static site: home (positioning), projects, writing, contact.
Hugging Face profile if you publish models or datasets.
LinkedIn headline consistent with the resume; about section short and specific.
A one-page PDF "portfolio index" for recruiters who will not click.
Pin exactly three repositories and archive the rest.
Audit your online presence for anything inconsistent with your positioning.
The recruiter screen: role fit, timeline, compensation band, work authorisation.
Referrals: the one-paragraph ask with a link to one artefact.
Warm intros via open-source work, talks, and mutual contacts.
Application tracking: a simple sheet with role, stage, contact, and next action.
Volume versus targeting: 20 well-targeted applications beat 200 sprays.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.7).** A recruiter can determine your fit from your resume and one link in under a minute.

sections.title: Writing and Visibility
sections.objective: Publish work that makes people want to talk to you.

items.text: Technical posts with a claim, evidence, and a reproducible artefact.
The negative-result post: what you tried, what failed, what you learned.
A reproducibility write-up: "I reproduced X and here is what broke".
Distribution: your site, a community, and one aggregator; not ten.
Consistency: one artefact per month beats a burst per year.
Responding to comments with data rather than defensiveness.
A monthly habit: ship, write, link, repeat.
Write one post about a failure, with numbers, and publish it.
Link every post back to a repository the reader can run.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.8).** You have at least two public write-ups, each tied to a runnable artefact.

sections.title: Open Source and Community
sections.objective: Earn credibility through contribution, not claims.

items.text: Choose libraries you actually use in your projects.
Start with documentation fixes, tests, and small bugs; then features.
Read the contribution guide; match the project's style.
Small, reviewable pull requests with a clear description.
Maintain one small thing of your own: an eval set, a utility, a dataset.
Community participation: answer questions where your users are.
Track contributions as portfolio evidence with links.
Land one merged pull request in a library you depend on.
Publish one small reusable artefact (dataset, eval set, utility) with a clear licence.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.9).** You have a merged contribution and a maintained artefact you can point to.

sections.title: Portfolio Review and Defence
sections.objective: Test the portfolio against hostile attention before interviewers do.

items.text: Recruit three reviewers: a peer, a senior engineer, and someone non-technical.
Give them a 15-minute task: "decide if you would interview this person".
Collect written feedback against the rubric; do not argue during review.
Fix the top three issues; ignore cosmetic preferences.
Rehearse the 30-second, 3-minute, and 15-minute versions of each project.
Prepare answers for the five questions every reviewer asks: why this, what baseline, what failed, what is the cost, what would you change.
Keep a changelog of portfolio improvements.
Run the review with three people and record every gap they found.
Re-run the review after fixes and compare.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (17.10).** Three reviewers independently reach "yes, interview" from the portfolio alone.

subBlocks.title: Project: `portfolio-pack` — three projects, three case studies, one flagship, one narrative

elements.text: Level 17 is complete when a hiring manager who has never spoken to you can defend your candidacy to their team.

items.text: I understand what a hiring manager does in the first pass.
I can select three projects that prove different things.
I can write a README that answers what, result, and how to run.

`portfolio-pack` passes every acceptance target.

I can defend any project at 30 seconds, 3 minutes, and 15 minutes.

elements.text: **Level 17 completion rule.** If your portfolio can get you the interview without you in the room, you are ready for Level 18.

levels.title: INTERVIEW PREPARATION
levels.goal: Convert knowledge into performance. Learn the loop, drill the rounds, rehearse under pressure, and turn offers into a decision you can defend.
levels.prerequisites: Level 17. Interviews are mostly a retrieval problem over work you have already done; you cannot retrieve what you never built.

dashboard.study commitment: 15–18 hrs/wk (2.5 hrs/day) part-time · ~2× faster full-time (30–35 hrs/wk)
dashboard.core tools: Your portfolio, a question bank, a timer, a recorder, mock partners
dashboard.main project: **`interview-war-room`** — drills, story bank, question ledger, two recorded mock loops
dashboard.final outcome: Pass applied-science and ML-engineer loops with prepared derivations, rehearsed designs, and measured project stories.

sections.title: Understanding the Loop
sections.objective: Know exactly what each round is testing so you prepare the right thing.

rows: coding, ML fundamentals, ML system design, production/debugging, behavioural
ML depth, ML coding, statistics & A/B, ML system design, research/project defence
coding, DL internals, distributed training, research discussion
SQL, statistics, case study, light ML, behavioural
coding, LLM fundamentals, RAG/agents design, evaluation, safety

items.text: Read the job description for the round structure before applying.
Map your three portfolio artefacts to the rounds they support.
Identify your weakest round early; it determines your prep allocation.
Take five real job postings and infer the likely loop for each.
Build a project-to-round map for your own portfolio.
Structure: can you organise an answer before speaking?
Depth: can you go one level below the buzzword?
Trade-offs: do you know what you gave up?
Measurement: do you quantify claims?
Communication: can a non-specialist follow you?
Ownership: can you say what you did versus what the team did?
Honesty: do you say "I do not know" cleanly?
Score yourself 1–5 on each dimension from your last three mock answers.
Pick the two weakest dimensions and design drills for them.
Six weeks: two weeks breadth (fundamentals), two weeks depth (your specialisation), two weeks simulation (mocks).
Daily: 10 fundamentals questions, 1 coding problem, 1 design or story.
Weekly: one full mock loop, one portfolio refinement, one written debrief.
Spaced repetition for derivations and definitions.
Track everything in a question ledger with confidence scores.
Write your six-week plan with hours per round and a weekly mock.
Set up a question ledger with 100 entries and initial confidence ratings.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.1).** You know your target role's loop, your weakest round, and the plan that addresses it.

sections.title: ML Fundamentals Drill
sections.objective: Answer any fundamentals question with a definition, a mechanism, and a trade-off.

items.text: The 100-question bank (Appendix A) as the backbone; add your own gaps.
Derive on paper: OLS, logistic gradient, softmax cross-entropy, attention, backprop for two layers, DDPM loss, DPO loss.
Explain each in 30 seconds, then in 3 minutes.
For every method: what it assumes, what it costs, when it fails.
Keep a ledger: question, confidence (1–5), last date, and where you learned it.
Revisit anything below 4 weekly; below 3, rebuild it from a reference.
Practise aloud; silent recall is not interview recall.
Answer 10 questions per day aloud and record the confidence after each.
Re-derive the five core formulas from memory every Monday.
Derive $\hat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$ and state the assumptions.
Derive the logistic regression gradient and explain $\hat p-y$.
Write scaled dot-product attention with shapes and the reason for $\sqrt{d_k}$.
Backpropagate through a two-layer ReLU network with cross-entropy.
State the DDPM objective and explain each term in one sentence.
Do all five in 25 minutes total, on a whiteboard, without notes.
Repeat weekly until each takes under four minutes.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.2).** You can deliver the five-minute whiteboard set cold, with correct shapes and one trade-off each.

sections.title: ML Coding Round
sections.objective: Implement models and utilities in NumPy under time pressure, with tests.

items.text: Implement: k-means, logistic regression with gradient descent, softmax, cross-entropy, top-k, AUC, precision/recall/F1, a confusion matrix, sampling with temperature, a moving average, one-hot encoding.
Implement attention and a minimal training step for an MLP.
Vectorise everything; avoid loops over samples.
Shape discipline: state shapes before coding.
Edge cases: empty input, single class, ties, NaNs, zero variance.
Test-first habit: check against a tiny known example before declaring done.
Narrate your approach before typing; silence reads as confusion.

elements.latex: \text{time budget}:\ 2\text{ min clarify}\ +\ 15\text{ min implement}\ +\ 3\text{ min test}

items.text: Implement three algorithms from scratch in 20 minutes each, with a test.
Do one session where you talk continuously through your reasoning.
Time yourself on each of the six; record where you lose minutes.
Redo the slowest two until both finish under 15 minutes.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.3).** Three algorithms implemented from scratch, tested, and explained, each within 20 minutes.

sections.title: SQL and Data Round
sections.objective: Handle the data questions that filter out strong modellers.

items.text: Joins, aggregations, window functions, CTEs, subqueries.
Ranking, running totals, month-over-month growth, cohort retention.
Deduplication and "latest record per entity" patterns.
Handling NULLs correctly in filters and joins.
Explaining a query plan and why an index matters.
Turning a vague product question into a query and stating assumptions.
Data-quality checks before trusting a result.
Solve 20 medium SQL problems, timed at 8 minutes each.
Write three retention-cohort queries from scratch and explain the grain.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.4).** You can answer a data question with a correct query and explain its grain and assumptions.

sections.title: Statistics and Experimentation Round
sections.objective: Defend an experiment design and an interpretation.

items.text: Power, MDE, and sample-size calculations by hand.
Interpreting confidence intervals and $p$-values correctly, in plain language.
Common traps: peeking, multiple comparisons, Simpson's paradox, regression to the mean.
CUPED and variance reduction.
A/B test design end to end: unit, metrics, guardrails, duration, analysis plan.
Causal questions: identification assumption, estimator, sensitivity.
Offline metric versus online outcome, and why gains fail to ship.
Design an A/B test for a ranking change in 10 minutes, aloud, with numbers.
Answer "the test shows +2% with $p=0.04$; do you ship?" in three different ways for three contexts.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.5).** You can design, size, and interpret an experiment without a calculator and without overclaiming.

sections.title: ML System Design Round
sections.objective: Run the seven-step frame under time pressure.

items.text: The seven-step frame from L16, rehearsed aloud against a timer.
Clarifying questions that change the design.
Back-of-envelope estimates within two minutes.
A drawn architecture with latency budgets per stage.
Failure modes and a degradation ladder.
Cost at three scales.
Handling follow-ups: 100× traffic, cold start, feedback loops, privacy.
Closing with risks and what you would measure first.
Two full 45-minute designs per week, recorded and debriefed.
One design where the interviewer interrupts every three minutes (train interruption tolerance).

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.6).** Three designs delivered aloud in 45 minutes each, with numbers and follow-ups handled.

sections.title: LLM and Applied AI Round
sections.objective: Show judgement about foundation-model systems, not enthusiasm.

items.text: When to prompt, when to retrieve, when to fine-tune — with cost and latency reasoning.
Evaluation methodology: your own eval set, judge calibration, regression suites.
RAG architecture and its failure modes, separated into retrieval versus generation.
Agents: tool schemas, step limits, cost ceilings, failure recovery.
Safety: injection, data exfiltration, output filtering, red-teaming.
Serving economics: tokens, caching, routing, quantisation.
A clear answer to "how would you halve the cost?" and "how do you know it is good?"
Prepare three "fine-tune or not" cases with numbers and a recommendation.
Present a RAG design in 15 minutes including the eval plan.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.7).** You can justify an LLM system decision with a measurement plan and a cost model.

sections.title: Project Deep-Dive and Behavioural
sections.objective: Tell project stories that survive follow-up questions.

items.text: 30-second, 3-minute, and 15-minute versions, rehearsed.
The five questions: why this, what baseline, what failed, what did it cost, what would you change.
Ownership clarity: your decisions versus the team's.
The one number you lead with, and why that number.
The diagram you can sketch in 60 seconds.
The failure you are willing to discuss, chosen deliberately.
Record the 3-minute version of each of your three projects.
Have a peer ask five hostile follow-ups per project; note where you wobble.
STAR, but with a metric: situation, decision, action, measured outcome.
Eight stories minimum: conflict, failure, ambiguity, influence, prioritisation, deadline pressure, disagreement with data, mentoring.
Each story under two minutes, with one number.
Avoid stories where you were simply right; show judgement under constraint.
Prepare the "why this company" answer with something specific and true.
Prepare the "tell me about yourself" in 90 seconds: past, present, why this role.
Write eight stories, each with a number, and rehearse two per day.
Ask a peer which story sounds rehearsed and which sounds real.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.8).** Eight story-bank entries with measured outcomes, plus three project deep-dives at three lengths.

sections.title: Take-Homes and Case Studies
sections.objective: Produce work that reads as senior in the time available.

items.text: Read the brief twice; list explicit and implicit requirements.
Timebox: 60–70% on the core, 20% on the write-up, 10% on polish, 10% reserve.
Baseline first; always show the trivial comparison.
A results table with an interval; a limitations section with a real limitation.
README with "how to run" and "what I would do with more time".
Do not over-engineer: scope discipline is part of the assessment.
Present the work in ten minutes with a clear recommendation.
Complete one take-home in a hard 8-hour box and note what you cut.
Present it to a peer in ten minutes and collect two criticisms.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.9).** A take-home with a baseline, an interval, and an honest limitations section, delivered inside the timebox.

sections.title: Mock Loops and Debriefs
sections.objective: Practise the whole loop, not just the parts you like.

items.text: Full loop: fundamentals → coding → statistics → design → project → behavioural.
Record every mock; the recording is the feedback, not your memory.
Debrief template: what was wrong, what was slow, what was unclear, what was missing.
Score each round 1–5 with evidence.
Fix the top three weaknesses with targeted reps before the next mock.
Mock with someone who will interrupt and push back.
Two full mocks minimum; three if your first was below 4/5.
Run a full recorded mock loop and score each round.
Repeat after two weeks and compare scores round by round.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.10).** Two recorded mock loops, each debriefed, with every round at 4/5 or above on the second attempt.

sections.title: Offers, Levelling and Negotiation
sections.objective: Make a decision you will not regret in a year.

items.text: Understand levels and bands: the same title means different scope at different companies.
Negotiate scope and level, not only base salary.
Components: base, bonus, equity (and its vesting and liquidity), sign-on, relocation.
Competing offers and the honest way to use them.
Evaluate the team: data access, whether models actually ship, mentorship, on-call load.
Ask about failure culture: how post-incidents are handled.
Read the offer carefully: IP, non-compete, and publication rights.
Decide on a framework you write down before the pressure arrives.

rows: What will I own in six months?
Do teams have access to the data they need?
What percentage of models reach production here?
Who reviews my work, and how often?
What is the on-call rotation and incident load?

items.text: Write your decision framework with weights before any offer arrives.
Role-play a negotiation with a peer and practise one specific ask.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (18.11).** A written decision framework and a rehearsed negotiation ask.

projects.title: Level 0 Capstone: ML Data Quality Toolkit
projects.tools: VS Code, Git, GitHub, terminal, `pytest`

elements.label: Purpose
elements.value: Build a reusable Python package that checks whether a dataset is ready for machine learning.

elements.text: This is far more useful than another calculator, because it introduces problems that return throughout the roadmap: data validation, missing values, incorrect types, reproducibility, error handling, and testing.

items.text: Load CSV files from a given path.
Report useful errors when a file does not exist.
Detect empty files and empty datasets.
Support a configurable delimiter and encoding.
Validate basic file-reading options.
Check whether required columns exist.
Report missing and unexpected columns.
Check column data types against an expected schema.
Count missing values per column.
Detect duplicate rows.
Report invalid numeric values (for example, `"N/A"` in an `age` column).
Support simple user-defined validation rules.
Report row and column counts.
Summarize numeric columns: count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max.
Summarize categorical columns: unique count, top values, frequency.
Calculate missing-value percentages.
Report duplicate counts.
Identify constant and near-constant columns.
Generate a readable summary report.
Organise the package into modules.
Add type hints and docstrings.
Create custom exceptions where useful.
Add unit tests.
Add logging.
Configure dependencies in `pyproject.toml`.
Add formatting and lint checks.
Create a GitHub repository.
Write complete installation instructions.
Provide a command-line interface.
Add continuous integration to run tests automatically.

projects.title: Level 1 Capstone: Vectorised Scientific Computing Library
projects.tools: NumPy, Pandas, Polars, DuckDB, Matplotlib, SciPy, PyTorch (tensors only)

subBlocks.title: Project: `sci-core` — a small NumPy-only scientific library

elements.text: **Purpose.** Re-implement the core numerical routines you will use for the rest of the roadmap, prove they are correct against trusted libraries, and prove they are fast.

items.text: Mean, median, variance, standard deviation, skewness, and quantiles.
Correct handling of `NaN` and of the $n$ versus $n-1$ convention.
Weighted versions of mean and variance.
Matrix multiplication without using `@` (loops first, then a vectorised version).
Solve $Ax=b$ via Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting.
LU decomposition; condition-number estimation.
Power iteration for the leading eigenvector; PCA via SVD.
OLS via normal equations, and via QR (numerically stable version).
Ridge regression with a closed-form solution.
Prediction with confidence intervals.
Stable softmax and log-sum-exp.
One-hot encoding and standardisation.
A seeded train/validation split.
A benchmark harness comparing each routine with NumPy/SciPy/sklearn.
Timing, memory, and maximum absolute difference for each comparison.
A single command that regenerates the results table.

elements.code:
sci-core/
├── src/sci_core/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── stats.py          # descriptive statistics, weighted versions
│   ├── linalg.py         # matmul, solve, LU, power iteration, PCA
│   ├── regression.py     # OLS (normal + QR), ridge
│   ├── numerics.py       # softmax, logsumexp, scaling, one-hot
│   └── benchmark.py      # correctness + timing harness
├── tests/
│   ├── test_stats.py
│   ├── test_linalg.py
│   ├── test_regression.py
│   └── test_numerics.py
├── benchmarks/
│   └── results.md        # generated table
└── README.md

items.text: Add `numba`-accelerated versions and report the speed-up.
Add `float32` support and quantify the accuracy loss.
Implement stochastic power iteration with convergence tolerance.
Profile the library and optimise the slowest routine.
Add a CLI: `sci-core describe data.csv --columns a,b,c`.

rows: Every routine tested against a trusted implementation with a stated tolerance.
Stability tests for softmax, log-sum-exp, and ill-conditioned systems.
Benchmark table with timings and ratios to NumPy/SciPy.
Clear module boundaries; no hidden global state.
Seeded results; one command regenerates benchmarks.
README explains each algorithm and its complexity.

elements.text: Level 1 is complete when all correctness targets pass **and** the benchmark table is reproducible from a clean clone.

projects.title: Level 2 Capstone: Maths Engine from Scratch

subBlocks.title: Project: `maths-engine` — autodiff, PCA, and optimisation in NumPy

elements.text: **Purpose.** Implement the mathematics you will use for the next sixteen levels, and prove each piece correct numerically. This project becomes your reference implementation for the rest of the roadmap.

items.text: `Tensor` class wrapping a NumPy array with `grad` and `requires_grad`.
Operations: add, subtract, multiply, divide, matmul, power, sum, mean, reshape.
Activations: sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, softmax.
Losses: MSE and cross-entropy.
A `backward()` that propagates gradients in reverse topological order.
Gradient checking for every op with relative error < $10^{-6}$ in float64.
Gram–Schmidt QR and Householder QR.
Power iteration and full eigen-decomposition for symmetric matrices.
SVD via eigen-decomposition of $A^\top A$ (with a note on its numerical limits).
PCA: fit, transform, inverse transform, and explained-variance ratio.
Gradient descent, momentum, Nesterov, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam.
Learning-rate schedules: constant, step, cosine, warmup + cosine.
A trainer that logs loss, gradient norm, and parameter norm per step.
Visualisation of training trajectories on a 2D loss surface.
Entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence, and mutual information.
Perplexity and label smoothing.

maths-engine/
├── src/maths_engine/
│   ├── tensor.py        # Tensor, op graph, backward pass
│   ├── ops.py           # elementwise + matmul operations
│   ├── nn.py            # Linear, activations, losses
│   ├── linalg.py        # QR, eigen, SVD, PCA
│   ├── optim.py         # SGD, momentum, Adam, schedules
│   └── info.py          # entropy, KL, perplexity
├── notebooks/
│   └── visualise_optimisers.ipynb
├── tests/
│   ├── test_gradients.py
│   ├── test_linalg.py
│   └── test_optim.py
└── README.md

rows: All ops pass gradient check, relative error $<10^{-6}$
Train to within $10^{-4}$ of the closed-form solution
Match `sklearn` accuracy within 0.5% on a small dataset
Trajectories match the mathematical update rules after 100 steps

items.text: Add forward-mode autodiff alongside reverse mode and compare costs.
Add a second-order optimiser (Newton or L-BFGS) for small problems.
Vectorise the autodiff engine's backward pass instead of looping over nodes.
Add a small `numba` kernel for the hottest operation and report the gain.
Plot loss-surface contours for a 2-parameter model with the optimiser trajectories overlaid.

rows: Every derivation in the README, every implementation tested numerically
All four parts implemented and demonstrated
Gradient checks, parity tests against NumPy/SciPy/sklearn
README explains each derivation in your own words
Optimiser trajectories clearly show the behavioural differences
Seeded runs; one command regenerates all figures and tables

elements.text: Level 2 is complete when all four parts work, all targets pass, and you can derive each result on a whiteboard without notes.

subBlocks.title: Project: `stats-infer` — inference, resampling, and an experiment study

elements.text: **Purpose.** Build the statistical toolbox you will reuse in every evaluation you run, and use it to answer a real question with defensible uncertainty.

items.text: Descriptive statistics with correct missing-data behaviour.
Standard errors: analytic, bootstrap, and jackknife.
Confidence intervals: normal, $t$, percentile bootstrap, basic bootstrap.
Hypothesis tests: one-sample and two-sample $t$, Welch, chi-square, Mann–Whitney, permutation.
Multiple-comparison corrections: Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini–Hochberg.
Power and sample-size calculators for proportions and means.
OLS with coefficient standard errors and $p$-values.
Robust (HC1) standard errors.
Bootstrap coefficient intervals.
Diagnostic plots generated automatically.
A configurable simulation harness: true effect, sample size, noise, test choice.
Run at least 1,000 replications per configuration.
Report bias, empirical standard error, coverage of the 95% interval, and power.
A results table and figure showing how each property changes with $n$ and effect size.
Pick one real question answerable with public data.
State the estimand, the identification assumption, and the analysis plan *before* analysing.
Report the effect with an interval, plus a sensitivity analysis.
Write a one-page memo with a recommendation.

elements.code:
stats-infer/
├── src/stats_infer/
│   ├── estimate.py      # SEs, CIs, bootstrap, jackknife
│   ├── tests_stats.py   # hypothesis tests + corrections
│   ├── power.py         # power and sample size
│   ├── regression.py    # OLS, robust SEs, diagnostics
│   └── simulate.py      # simulation harness
├── reports/
│   ├── simulation_study.md
│   └── experiment_memo.md
├── figures/
└── tests/

rows: Empirical coverage within 1.5% of nominal at $n=100$
Interval matches SciPy's bootstrap to within Monte Carlo error
Simulated power within 2% of the analytic calculation
1,000+ replications per cell, Monte Carlo error reported

items.text: Add a Bayesian estimation module (conjugate models and a simple Metropolis sampler).
Add sequential testing (always-valid $p$-values).
Add CUPED variance reduction to the experiment analysis.
Build a CLI: `stats-infer power --baseline 0.10 --mde 0.02`.
Publish the experiment memo as a blog-style report.

rows: Simulation study shows calibrated coverage, not just point accuracy
Each method documented with its assumptions
One real analysis with a pre-stated plan and a sensitivity analysis
Seeded simulation; one command regenerates the report

elements.text: Level 3 is complete when the toolkit passes its targets **and** the simulation study demonstrates that your intervals actually cover at the nominal rate.

projects.title: Phase 1 Capstone — FOUNDATIONS LAB
projects.tools: VS Code, Git + GitHub, terminal, `uv`, `pytest`, NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Jupyter

elements.text: **Purpose.** Prove the four levels work *together*. A single repository that ingests messy data, computes with vectorised code, models it with maths you implemented yourself, and reports results with correct uncertainty.
**Suggested duration.** 1–2 weeks **Depends on.** Levels 0, 1, 2, and 3.

Pick **one real question** answerable with a public dataset — ideally one you care about (credit default, hospital readmission, crop yield, exam performance, electricity demand, IPL outcomes, anything with a defensible outcome variable).
Then produce:

items.text: **A package** — not a notebook — that loads, validates, cleans, and models the data.
**A from-scratch estimator** — logistic or linear regression implemented with your own autodiff from Level 2, with gradients derived in the README.
**A statistical claim** — an effect, a difference, or a prediction with an interval attached, and the assumptions stated.
**A decision memo** — one page, written for someone who will act on the result.
**A reproducible report** — one command regenerates every number and figure.

rows: Schema checks, missingness report, duplicate detection, typed columns
No Python loops over rows; a benchmark table before/after
Trivial baseline, a library model, and your implementation, side by side
Bootstrap or analytic interval on every headline number

elements.text: **Purpose.** Run a complete mini research project end-to-end: a question, a protocol, an artefact, a result, a critique, and a paper-style writeup. This is the artefact that most directly predicts success in an applied-science interview.
